utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. O'Sullivan will now continue. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe the bundle of exhibits has now been placed in front of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday when we broke we were talking about Rambouillet, and the first exhibit I'd like to discuss with you is 1D18, e-court pages 418 to 425. And for you in hard copy it's tab 33. This again is taken from the compilation of materials from Professor Weller's book. And you'll see there, Ambassador, that as a copy of the Rambouillet agreement as it existed on the 6th of February, 1999, and we see there that there's -- there are four components to it. There's a framework agreement, annex 1 on the constitution, annex 3 on elections, and annex 4 the ombudsman and I believe you were explaining during your direct examination that over the period of the Rambouillet talks, there were a couple of things. And the first is we notice here that the segments or elements are called annexes and later I believe you said they became chapters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And as time progressed different elements of the agreement were tabled between the 6th and 23rd; correct, different chapters?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the final version, which is the 23rd of February, which we'll come to later this morning, has a total of nine chapters and I think you would agree with me that the chapters are numbered 1 through 8 but there is an annex 4(A) which makes a total of 9 chapters in the final agreement. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would to double-check, but yeah, I'd have to look at it and I guess you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Fine. We'll move --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can state to you that that's --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- correct, but we'll come back to that. Now, these annexes or chapters, as they were later called, were tabled by the negotiators, you the negotiators, on behalf of the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in Exhibit P2658 which is the final report that you sent to Vienna on the 25th of February you said this, and I'll just read it to you. You said: "Negotiations" -- this is your final report where you're summarising the events that took place at Rambouillet and it's sent on the 25th of February 1999. You say: "Negotiations with the Contact Group took up more time than the negotiations between the parties to the conflict. Some annexes were only agreed to upon internally at a very late date and therefore only reached the parties at a late stage." And I think this confirms the fact that you were tabling these chapters on behalf of the Contact Group; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that during the first week, and I would put it on the 12th of February, that you received a letter from Professor Markovic, the head of delegation, requesting that his delegation be given all relevant documents that were to be discussed at -- during the talks. Does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not distinctly recall the letter, but I do recall the discussion about the way forward. It was reached agreement in the Contact Group that we should proceed in such a way that we hand out chapter after chapter in order to make progress and in order not to confuse and in order to be able to focus and take this step-by-step approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at Exhibit 1D96, that's tab 34 for you, Ambassador. It's the letter that Professor Markovic sent to you, Tab 34, 1D96. It should be the next document in your bundle, tab 34.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 34 starts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's a very short letter and I think it confirms what you just said, that it was sent to the negotiators by Professor Markovic as head and it's simply asking -- we're in the first week and he just requests the -- all the relevant documents intended for discussions and I think your explanation has put light on the context of this letter. Does this letter does -- seeing it now, does it refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Professor Markovic also approached you, the negotiators, requesting to organise face-to-face meetings with the Albanian delegation also, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. After the refusal on the part of the Yugoslav delegation to meet with the Kosovar Albanians in the initial phase, which I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That was the opening ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opening ceremonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Where they were not comfortable sitting down with the KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Albanian delegation as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But the central complaint was the fact that KLA was there; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, there was also a request by Mr. Markovic on behalf of his delegation, which I believe you mentioned yesterday or the day before, that both delegations sign the non-negotiable basic principles or the basic elements issued by the Contact Group on the 30th of January, 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we never saw those elements during your direct examination and 1D18, e-court page 414, tab 35 in hard copy, if you see tab 35 in the left-hand column at the bottom, "Contact Group non-negotiable principles, basic elements, 30 January 1999." You recognise that as the basic principles?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that is the document that the Serb/Yugoslav delegation was asking to be signed?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe yesterday you said in reference to P2662, which is a dispatch you sent your foreign ministry on the 10th of February that this demand was dropped on the 10th of February after Foreign Ministers Cook and Vedrine and the mediators gave their assurances that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY would be preserved. That's what you said a couple of days ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, of course, we see that one of the elements of the basic elements was the territorial integrity of the FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe you said also that it was quite a legitimate concern, given the fact that as a state delegation that would be one of their interests in preserving their sovereignty and territorial integrity; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, a more general question about these things we've just discussed here very briefly. Would it be fair to say that requesting a face-to-face meeting and having both sides sign the basic principles and requesting all documents is -- can be seen as a constructive request. I mean, it would be a sign of good well, confidence-building measure. It's nothing other than an attempt to facilitate the discussions. Would that be a fair way to put it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. The signing of the non-negotiable principles was deemed not necessary by the Contact Group because of the fact, as I already mentioned, that it was included in the invitation to both sides. So we deemed it not necessary to waste time on the signing ceremony, on the difficulties to get the two groups together. We saw how difficult it was to organise the first inaugural meeting to be in the same room and so on. We only had one week originally; therefore, we had to move on and we could not allow the procrastination and side-stepping in terms of a signing ceremony which was obsolete, because it was already a pre-condition for both parties to appear in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. I'll just stop you there, because perhaps my question was too general. I'm not disputing that it was in your prerogative as the negotiators to make those discussions, but the requests in and of themselves were not unreasonable. They could have been constructive -- seen as constructive requests to meet -- to meet face-to-face, to have all the documents and to sign the basic agreement?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances with parties who are cooperative, that would not have been a big deal. Under those circumstances, it was a big deal; therefore, the Contact Group arrived at the decision not to engage in this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I accept that. Thank you. P2793 is the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic case. You don't have that in hard copy, Ambassador, I just made reference to it for the record. P2793 is the transcript and at page 7726 [sic] I'll read what you said about -- about the Serb FRY delegation at Rambouillet. You said: "Once things started to roll on both sides there was a very constructive phase with the Yugoslav side experts taking over, so to speak, from the politicians negotiating. Hammering out compromised solutions, proposals that were in -- then in turn passed on to the Albanian side, the Kosovo Albanians dealt with it and it came back and so on." That was your testimony in Milosevic, and I think it's a fair summary of the way it was working in that period in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know that Mr. Milutinovic arrived at Rambouillet near the end of the first week, which would be Thursday, the 11th of February; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a recollection when he actually arrived, but he was there in Paris, yes, and then also in Rambouillet later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you with that then. Again it's the Milosevic transcript P2793, page 7221, line 10, I'll just read it back to you to refresh your memory. You said: "Later on, around 11 February," which I say is Thursday, "the Serbian president, Mr. Milutinovic, arrived. He stayed in Paris and also served as an informal point of contact, obviously, for -- for the Rambouillet delegation, Yugoslav/Serb delegation, and then later on occasionally dropped by and became more involved -- more and more engaged and involved; however, on a more political level when it came to contacts with the Contact Group foreign ministers who were chaperoning, so to speak, these negotiations." Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you emphasise a couple of things here. You say Mr. Milutinovic serving as a point of contact and his engagement on a political level at Rambouillet. This is much the same role he played throughout 1998 and it's much the same relationship he had with Mr. Markovic's delegation in 1998, is it not? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you knew that Mr. Milutinovic had been SFRY and FRY ambassador to Greece from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew that he had been the FRY foreign minister before becoming -- being elected president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've met him in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew that he -- that Mr. Milutinovic knew and had previously worked with many of the Contact Group foreign ministers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would it be -- is it also correct to say that Mr. Milutinovic was not the only political figure from Yugoslavia who was not a member of the delegation who was present, either at Rambouillet or later in Paris; and I'm thinking in particular of Vuk Draskovic, who at the time was the deputy prime minister of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you may also recall that Mr. Jovanovic, the foreign minister of the FRY at the time, was also appearing from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't recall, in fact, but it -- if you have researched this, then it should be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But do you recall seeing or knowing that the foreign minister would come either to Rambouillet or to Paris?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I do not recall this. Of course, I have met foreign minister on several occasions, but I do not recall whether -- where -- whether I have met him in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Fine. But the people like -- that you did see from outside the delegation, the political figures, typically at this -- these meetings, they were there to meet and speak to individuals in connection with these ongoing -- the ongoing process; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, going to the second week of the meetings, and I'm thinking in particular of Tuesday, the 16th of February, which is the Tuesday of that second week. The negotiators, you were presented with comprehensive comments and responses from both delegations. Would you -- I can show you a document in connection to that, but that sound right that at the beginning of the second week?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sounds right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the next document I would like to look at is e-court 1D18, pages 431 to 438. And, Ambassador, you have that at tab 36. We've looked at the first draft of the Rambouillet Accord on the 6th of February. Here on -- at 1D18, tab 36, we have the second draft dated the 18th of February. Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this was the draft that was prepared after you had received these comprehensive comments and responses from both delegations on the 16th; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we see here that at the very beginning of this document that there is preamble included which was not in the first draft; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We see that the framework is still there, that's just below the preamble. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you turn the page we now see in the left-hand column near the bottom: "Chapter 1: Constitution." As we've said -- as we've agreed the annexes are now called chapters; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you turn over -- that's the second page, third, fourth, the fifth page, you'll see that there's a chapter 3. So if you keep turning you'll see chapter 3. In the hard copy up at the top right-hand corner it should be page 439. Top right-hand corner of your -- it's the pagination from the book, go to page 439 in hard copy. Do you see that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's chapter 3, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the left lower corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's right. So chapter 3 is the elections. If you turn to the next page, please, we see a new chapter on the next page, chapter 4.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Economic issues.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In that same page chapter 4(A), which is also new, humanitarian assistance, reconstruction, and economic development.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Still on the same page, chapter 6, the ombudsman. And if you turn over to the next page we have chapter 8, which is new: "Amendments, comprehensive assessment, and final clauses." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have a document I'd like to hand to the Bench and to the Prosecution, and I'm going to seek your leave to use it. But I would like you to see the document and I would make a submission to you on it, and so if I could ask that a copy be given to the Bench and to the Prosecutor for the time being. Your Honour, this is a table which I prepared. I don't -- if you allow me to use it -- I'll tell you the reasons why I'd use it. The left-hand column, the first column, represents the elements of the agreement as it existed on the 6th of February. The middle column shows the elements of the agreement on the 18th. And in the third column, which you haven't come to is the -- all the elements of the agreement, and I'm trying to juxtapose them to it's clear to the witness and anyone following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you a problem with that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In that case, could I ask the usher once again to give the Ambassador a copy and place a copy on the ELMO for the public. Your Honour, I believe if we're going to use this document, it may become part of the record and can it be given an IC number now, just for identification purposes at least.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, this table you have in front of you is a document that I produced and I can represent to you that I believe it's a faithful reproduction of the elements of the Rambouillet agreement as it evolved over time. And starting with the first column on the far left we have the four elements of the February 6th agreement, the framework, the constitution, ammendments, and ombudsman. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the middle column are the elements of the 18th and you see the preamble is added, chapters 4 and 4(A), and 8 are added. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We'll deal with the third column later, because that's the comprehensive agreement, and a few moments ago I was suggesting to you that there were, in fact, nine chapters, if you look at the far right, because they're numbered 1 through 8 but there's a chapter 4A, which means, in fact, nine chapters. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But we'll come back to that. So we're dealing with the Rambouillet agreement as it existed on the 18th of February with the contents we have there in front of us. Now P2661 is an e-mail dispatch you sent to your foreign ministry on the 18th of February. You looked at that yesterday with my learned friend Mr. Stamp, and I'll just remind you what you said in that. This dispatch is the 18th of February and you wrote: "The new draft agreement was revised on 17th February at the Contact Group expert level -- the Contact Group without the Russian Federation and finished in consultation with the Russian Federation in the night between the 17th and 18th of February." So this is the document that we're talking about that resulted from that process; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then you wrote in this same dispatch to your foreign ministry: "It was presented to the parties on 18 February with the instruction to consider it final. The draft made concessions to the Serbian side on points which it considered to be of -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, just a moment. Which tab number is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's not -- I don't think it's in the tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, right. Sorry, sorry. I was looking in the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not on the screen either, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Can we have -- can we put P2661 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My apologies, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. It's the bottom of the second page, please. Well, English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, Ambassador, we'll use the English.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well -- perhaps the Bench understands German, but I would be a little hard-pressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. There you have the segment of the dispatch you sent, and I was just reading it to you, that the new -- you've confirmed the first part of that bullet point that this document produced on the 18th was the result of the process on the 17th and 18th among the Contact Group members, which you undertook after you received the comprehensive comments by both parties. It was in the middle of that bullet point that I said: "The draft made concessions to the Serbian side on points which it considered to be of particular importance (see above), without making any substantial changes. A two-chamber system was established, giving the second chamber a merely advisory role. The ties with the Serbia/FRY and the stressing the issue of sovereignty were conceded by adding a preamble to the constitution." So this is the comment you sent to Vienna regarding the draft of the 18th of February; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, when you say you consider it final in this paragraph -- I'm sorry, you sent it to Vienna, not to Serbia, your dispatch.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you say in this paragraph that you consider -- that the parties should consider it the final agreement, of course what we're -- what you mean, I believe, is that it's the final political components of the Rambouillet agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's a reference, of course, to the political part of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. Because the implementation components come later?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. The next exhibit I'd like to look at is P563, P563, which is tab 37. P563, tab 37, which is your e-mail dispatch to Vienna on the 19th of February at 1300 hours. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the dispatch is 19th -- yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The dispatch is 19th, yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I'm looking there at the third paragraph where you say: "On 18 February at 1900 hours the Yugoslav/Serb delegation presented its provisional opinion, noting that the draft had been improved but not indicating any change of position." Would it be fair to say that at this point your understanding was that the Serb delegation was in basic -- basic agreement with the political components, but for the points that they were highlighting here in your memo?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our feeling at the time was that clearly -- I mean, you could go on forever to make points where we would like to have this or that changed. Yeah. But the feeling was that the Serb/Yugoslav delegation, in fact, was ready to accept the political part, those parts that we had so far thoroughly negotiated and also were backed by the whole Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Also in this dispatch at the bottom of the first page we read: "On the evening of 18 February the Albanians voiced their bitter disappointment with the new draft. Their cooperativeness had been abused and Serbian obstinacy rewarded. Representatives of the delegation handed in a written protest in which they recorded their rejection of the final draft." So the Albanians actually sent to you a written protest. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If we can go to Exhibit 1D18, e-court 441, 442. 1D18, 441, 442.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's tab 38, Ambassador, from the Weller book. What you have in front of you is the Kosova delegation statement on new proposal for a settlement dated 18 February 1999. I'd like to look at a couple of aspects of this with you. Let's start with the first paragraph, the last couple of sentences. It says: "The delegation of Kosova returns this document to the Contact Group, as it is unacceptable for consideration at this late stage. In fact, it represents a breach of faith by the Contact Group."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, can you see the -- have you found --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 17, Kosova delegation statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. Okay. There is -- the first paragraph is there beginning "the Kosova delegation has studied."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In that same paragraph if you go down four lines --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- you see what I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if you go down that column near the bottom you see a heading "the issue of sovereignty and legal status" underlined, correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Go up there from there several lines and there's a sentence beginning with the word "hence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it says: "Hence the delegation of Kosovo returns the new draft on the political aspects of the settlement to the negotiators as procedurally and substantively unacceptable document." Then we get into one of the complaints, which comes under the heading, as you see underlined there "the issue of sovereignty and legal status." And again I'll just read briefly the first paragraph. "The first point relates to the insertion of the word 'sovereignty' into the preamble on annex 1." Now, at this point you have inserted the word "sovereignty" into the preamble of the agreement haven't you? We've seen that.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in from the outset, in fact--

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but not there in the -- not there in the preamble and other parts of -- I guess I -- all in all, there's three times a reference in there to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia in the whole Rambouillet Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And continuing on it says: "This is made even worse by the formal declaration that the authorities of governance set forth in the agreement originate from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This action is fundamentally inconsistent with the understanding that a settlement would be without prejudice to the status of Kosovo in the interim period." And if we could turn over to the next page, I'm looking at the left-hand column. And if go down to the second full paragraph which begins: "The Kosovo delegation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "The Kosovo delegation will not countenance a total change to the character of the agreement at the last movement, even if it is achieved through the insertion of a single word. Moreover, the proposal that the rights and powers of Kosova are derived from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is similarly conceptually incompatible with the approach that was taken by the Contact Group and the conference from the very beginning of the talks." And the last part I would like to highlight is the following paragraph: "It is the position of the delegation of Kosova that a referendum on the further status of Kosova must be held after the expiry of an interim period. Again, a reference to sovereignty would constrain the delegation of Kosova to insist on a far clearer formation of the obligation to hold a referendum in the concluding provisions of the framework interim agreement than might have been contemplated otherwise." And there there's -- I won't continue to read, but you can see they're talking -- the complaint is to the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the FRY; correct? You see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, yes, I've seen it. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you recall that on the 10th of February the two co-chairs of the conference and the negotiators gave assurances to the FRY/Serb delegation that signing the basic principles wasn't necessary because sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY would be preserved. Now, was this pointed out to the Kosovar delegation by you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. And what was their reaction to that --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When they were told it was non-negotiable and it would be preserved, what did they say?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I think it is -- we need to recall that the summoning of the two sides to Rambouillet had a very clear framework, and that was no independence but a high degree of autonomy. So from the outset both sides knew there's not going to be a separation of Kosovo from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Kosovar Albanian side of course also knew that they are not negotiating independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this was made clear to the Kosovar delegation after you received this response from them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn then to the 20th of February, that's the Saturday, which originally, as we have said, was supposed to be the last day of the conference, correct, Saturday, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On that day, the 20th, the foreign ministers of the Contact Group met with representatives of both delegations; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there the basic question that the foreign ministers had for the delegations was whether they accepted the political framework; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this meeting took place at Rambouillet in a room on the main floor of the castle where the foreign ministers sat at a long table and the negotiators were there and I think your aides and interpreters were all together in this room; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It might have looked a bit like this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Smaller. And if you were sitting at the table as one of the representatives of the negotiating team, you might at this point understand that all eyes and ears are focused on you. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the three of us and the foreign ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And both delegations were called in one by one; in other words, they -- the Albanian delegation came in first and later, after a pause, the Serb/FRY delegation came in; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, do you --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the head of the delegation. I do not recall now distinctly whether it was the whole delegation or just part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was representatives of each delegation.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And roughly speaking, can you give an approximation of how long did the meeting with the Albanian delegation last that morning, roughly speaking? Was it 10 minutes? 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not really recall the meeting inside the room. It was clearly -- there were already meetings outside of the room, preparatory meetings in particular with the head of the delegation, with the head of the delegations, and then in the room itself it was, of course, a high-wire atmosphere, and so time flew. I do not -- I cannot really recall now whether it was one hour or two hours all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, all together being -- both --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But the Albanian delegation came in first; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And as you said -- I've been misspeaking -- it's representatives of the delegation came in. And to refresh your memory, the delegation Albanian representatives were Mr. Thaqi, the late Dr. Rugova, Mr. Surroi, and Mr. Qosja. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, of course, Mr. Thaqi was the head of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Thaqi spoke, and the more he spoke the more it became apparent to you that he was not -- that he was going to say no to the agreement and isn't it true that at one point you and Chris Hill looked at each other and you knew that it wasn't going to work, that Mr. Thaqi wasn't going to say yes?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a fascinating situation, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But, sir, is that -- do you recall him --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, I don't recall, but it was -- one could see how a 30-year-old guy just taken in from the mountains into this conference room, thinking he -- this will be his big hour all of a sudden realised that he would have to sign up to the dissolution of the very organisation that he has helped to found. So the pressure was simply too big for him and he could not come up with a straight yes or a straight no.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when this became apparent, the Contact Group ministers got more and more nervous, and in particular, the Italian foreign minister, Mr. Dini stated that under these circumstances one cannot negotiate. Didn't he say that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then Mr. Cook spoke up, speaking to Mr. Hashim Thaqi, he said: Hashim, are you -- what you are saying here means no. That's what Mr. Cook said, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not recall distinctly, but it could have been this way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And to that Mr. Thaqi said: No, it's not no, but it's not yes, either; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Cook replied to Thaqi: That means it could be yes, but something is missing; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a good interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there was at that point great confusion and then an adjournment was called; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you've -- what I've taken you through Mr. -- Ambassador Petritsch, is almost verbatim what you told Brook Lapping, a subsidiary of the BBC?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can read it back to you, but I can tell you what I have faithfully put to you what you told Brook Lapping when you sat down with him and gave him an interview on videotape --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Must have been in 1999? Must have been 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it could have been. I don't have the date, but for the record, it's Exhibit 1D207. Do you have any reason to dispute what I've just put to you--

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- or should I read the transcript again?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sure this is basically along the lines of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you said that prior to the meeting, this meeting in the morning, you had actually sat down with Mr. Thaqi and on the basis of that short meeting in the morning of the 20th with Mr. Thaqi, you expected him to say yes to the agreement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting -- there were several meetings, as I have indicated, and one of the meetings was with -- together with the foreign minister Fischer, Joschka Fischer. Since Mr. Thaqi speaks German, it was easier for us to talk to him in German. And so we sat down and went through with him. Obviously, he was not -- up to then, he did not grasp the whole complexity and the consequences of what is happening here, that there is not going to be just one part, the part that they like, but that there are also other parts in the agreement that are part and parcel of the whole agreement and only the whole agreement can be signed and not just cherry-picking and picking and choosing. That was basically what we wanted to impress on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. And I was, quite precisely, thinking of the short meeting you had with Mr. Thaqi and Mr. Fischer just before this meeting with the Contact Group ministers, and that's why you had the impression that Mr. Thaqi was going to say yes; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he, as always, never really expressed himself in a clear way, but I -- we had the feeling that he understood what is at stake and that we need a clear answer from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you know that on the 19th, the day before, Mr. Thaqi and Mr. Morten Abramovic, one of the expert consultants to the Albanian delegation, flew to Ljubljana to meet with Mr. Demaqi; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when Mr. Thaqi returned from Ljubljana, didn't he have a meeting with you and Ambassador Hill saying that he would approve the entire agreement before the 20th of February deadline?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not -- the deadline or the date was not really part of the talk, but he indicated that he would be able to sign at a meeting with Demaqi, who was against this agreement, was a positive one, and thus we assumed that he would be able to say yes to the political part.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, your -- my colleague here will find the -- he will find the correspondence you sent to Vienna where I put to you that you said to Vienna that you and Ambassador Hill had met with Mr. Thaqi after he returned from Ljubljana and he promised you he would accept the agreement before the 20th of February deadline. I can pull that out if you want, but do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about what I said. I do not recall now exactly after seven years what the words were, but basically it was positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. You also know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say there that Demaqi was against the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Previously was protesting he did not join the Kosovar Albanian delegation. They wanted to have him on board, but he was against it from the outset, but then obviously, in this talk in Ljubljana between Thaqi and Demaqi, Demaqi then changed his mind and was, according to Mr. Thaqi, in support of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Again on the 19th of February, that's the Friday, the Friday before this Contact Group -- Contact Group summoned the delegations, you know that members of the Kosovar delegation were permitted to leave the castle to meet with General Wesley Clark to discuss military and security issues, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you're aware of it --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now that this happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How could it be that you were a Contact Group representative and negotiator and you didn't know that this was taking place? Can you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's easily explained, because that was the military part and for the military part the NATO experts were in charge and, as I said on another occasion, that was primarily with the American negotiator, Chris Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what they were discussing were, in fact, what eventually became annexes 2, 5, and 7; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the purpose of this exercise was --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- the matters that were discussed were what eventually became the implementation portions of the Rambouillet Agreement, chapters 2, 5, and 7 that was what was discussed with General Clark?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were already -- of course, they were already finalised, and what the purpose of meeting was was to inform them, since they were not formally a party to the military agreement, clearly, because this can only be a government, they got the information from General Clark what about the content of the implementation and security chapters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these -- they don't appear in your middle column here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, because they were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not -- are you accepting the proposition that's just been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were not -- they were not part of the 18th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're saying here they were already finalised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Internally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean by the Contact Group and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. By the NATO experts and -- but not yet formally endorsed by the Contact Group because of the fact that Russia clearly always was waiting until there was consensus on the part of the Yugoslav side to anything that was negotiated, and only then afterwards, Russia adjoined the consensus in the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That fits. It's just the use of the expression "finalised" wasn't clear, but it's now clear, I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, the point being that these -- although the texts were finalised, they were not incorporated into the agreement until the 23rd, not on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is that correct, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And just to -- so now we have Mr. Thaqi has gone to Ljubljana. Members of the Kosovar delegation have met with General Clark. And just moving ahead, I hope it doesn't break the chronology too much, on the 23rd of February Mr. Milo, the foreign minister of Albania, was in Rambouillet meeting with the Kosovar delegation, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you received a protest letter from Professor Markovic complaining about Mr. Milo being in the castle; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, why was he allowed in the castle when you told us yesterday that you know -- that you knew that the Republic of Albania was furnishing organisation, recruitment, and training for the KLA? Why was that person from a foreign state who supported the KLA allowed in?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not -- I was not saying for sure that this -- they -- that this was happening through the Government of Albania. But I knew and I indicated that it was happening from the territory of Albania. But the role of Mr. Milo, of course, was to encourage the Kosovo Albanian side to sign up to the Contact Group Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The -- let's go back to the exchange where Mr. Thaqi is not saying yes and Mr. -- Foreign Minister Dini and Foreign Minister Cook intervened. And I said to you -- I put it to you that Robin Cook said that the answer is, yes, but something is missing. But the thing that was missing for Mr. Thaqi was the referendum; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically what -- now I cannot interpret poor Mr. Cook but what he -- at the time, my impression was that what was missing was a clear yes or a clear no. It was this kind of maybe yes but I don't know, and that was not enough for everybody to convince us that there is an unambiguous yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the part that was missing, the reason that Mr. Thaqi could not say yes is that there was no referendum? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's explore that. We've just looked at the statement from the Kosovo delegation where they're demanding explicit reference to a referendum; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Exhibit P2260 is your e-mail dispatch of 22 February, 0900 hours. We don't have it in hard copy but it's P2260 -- I'm sorry, it is tab 39. P2260 is --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 39, yeah.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So this is written two days after this meeting with the Contact Group foreign ministers. And there you write in relation to -- in the first paragraph, middle of the first paragraph, you're talking about the events in Rambouillet taking a turn for the worse. And you write: "Nothing has changed on the now-stubborn stance on the referendum issue evident since Saturday morning." You did know about this?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the referendum --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you said no to me a moment ago, that's why I --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was a misunderstanding. It was very clear from the outset, there were several points that were absolutely clear. The Yugoslav side did not want a separation from Kosovo, from the state; so therefore, sovereignty and territorial integrity, that was their position. The second position on the part of Yugoslavia was the presence of military international military presence, that was the second point of contention. And on the side of the Albanians, it was the issue of independence and a referendum and the KLA. They wanted to preserve the KLA, they wanted to get independence, and they wanted to have a referendum for this independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to keep this in mind, one always needs to keep this in mind and it goes back and forth and back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if your question was entirely fair when you read the next sentence of the dispatch. "It's becoming increasingly clear that the real reason for the intransigence was the dissolution of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that there -- the ambassador said there was two reasons: There's the referendum issue and the dissolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but he's disputing your contention that Thaqi would not say yes because there was no referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You put a question to him based on only that part of the dispatch, which I don't think, in the circumstances, was entirely fair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it is clear that he is one of the KLA leaders. The dissolution of the KLA was the toughest point in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll return to this matter later, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, then I'd like to look at this issue. You say what the KLA wanted was independence and not autonomy or substantial self-government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was their ultimate goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now just --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just by the KLA, by the way, that was the stated goal of all of each and every Kosovo leader and probably whatever, 89 per cent of the Kosovar Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's go back -- let's go back to your testimony yesterday when we were discussing 1998. And I put to you that the reason why the Albanians never answered the numerous and quite legitimate invitations from both Professor Markovic and, from time to time, from Mr. Milutinovic is because they didn't want to negotiate autonomy or self government; they wanted independence?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right, and this is the reason why the international community decided to mediate, because we realised that the Yugoslav side alone will never manage to find a viable compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always misunderstood of something being on the one side. We were always in foreign equitable solution and we increasingly more realised there is not going to be a direct bilateral agreement between Belgrade and Pristina possible. That's the rationale behind the engagement of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So here we are in Rambouillet in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just going back slightly to your answer about the goal of every Kosovo leader, at least the stated goal of every Kosovo leader. That would apply at that stage also to Rugova?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And already way before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well -- so now we are in 1999, in Rambouillet, under the auspices of the Contact Group, international group, and the Kosovar -- and nothing changes. Do you -- the Kosovar position is still the same, they want independence, they don't care about autonomy or self government. They want independence, they want a referendum guaranteeing them independence. So nothing has changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing has changed that, through the mediation, we have provided an agreement which prevents independence, which does not grant independence to Kosovo. That's the main difference, which obviously was not something that Belgrade was able to achieve earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Every proposal of Ambassador Hill in 1998 and every proposal from Belgrade in 1998 did the same thing, it didn't give independence to Kosovo, it gave substantial autonomy and self government, it preserved territorial integrity and sovereignty, the same as you're saying you did?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And what happened in the meantime and in parallel -- we have to always sort of get the feedback from the ground, and on the ground violence escalated. That was the big problem. And that clearly demonstrated up to the 15th of January with Racak that there is no solution in direct talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: After the -- going back to the 20th, after there was an adjournment, after the meeting between the Contact Group foreign ministers and the Albanian delegation, the Serb/FRY delegation was summoned to is that room as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And certain representatives of the Serb and the FRY came, including Mr. Milutinovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not now recall who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you recall that Mr. Milutinovic was there?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Don't you recall that Mr. Milutinovic spoke to the foreign ministers of the Contact Group and said, "We basically agree with political agreement"?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're helping me on my feet. I think that this was the way you just described it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I realise you're covering lots of material and maybe I should help you more often. P2792, you don't have it there, it's your interview with the Prosecutor and I'll just remind you what you said on page 4. It's an exhibit. It's from your interview with the OTP. You said: "The Serb delegation worked substantively and we made significant progress by agreeing to a compromise political and legal system for Kosovo. Even Milutinovic said that the Contact Group foreign ministers on 19th February, that the Serbs could live with the political aspects of the proposed agreement."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think the date is wrong. It is actually Saturday the 20th, but --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was already a meeting but Mr. Milutinovic should know this better, I guess, than me. There was also a meeting, informal meetings on the sides, and on the 19th in the evening I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of May, 1999, and on the 9th of June, 1999, and that's Exhibit P792 [sic]. If you can bring that up. P792. I believe you had a chance to review this before you testified. You came into court and you said that you adopted this statement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you can see the dates on the cover page, 14 May and 9 June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that's approximately three or four months after Rambouillet; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed by the Prosecutor, you used your best efforts to give a detailed and accurate account during those two meetings with the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you spoke about events and individuals as you remembered them. Would that be a fair way to put it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3, please. I don't think we need the German, although, I'm sure the Ambassador -- that's the Serbian, I'm sorry. All right, the middle paragraph there, beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll read it to you: "Vladimir Stambuk, the representative from the Yugoslav party of the left, JUL, was well educated but the most unsavory of the group. At one point, he and I were discussing various alternatives to the Kosovo conflict and he said to me, If NATO bombs fall, there will be a massacre in Kosovo." Then you said: "He did not qualify this statement, but my first and distinct impression was to interpret that as a direct threat to the Albanians. He was not referring to the fact that NATO bombs would lead to large-scale deaths in Kosovo, rather, he meant that a NATO attack would result in a massacre of the Albanian population by Serbian forces. He stated this as if it were an un -- an unequivocal fact. I was quite taken aback by this statement and it made a distinct impression on me." Now, did you know Mr. Stambuk before Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have met him, but I do not have any recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you say that when he made this statement, you were quite taken aback and it made a distinct impression on you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we can see the emphasis on this statement -- I mean if -- it's the line, "If NATO bombs fall, there will be a massacre in Kosovo." It's centred, it's in bold, and the word "will" is underlined; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, nowhere in this statement, nowhere in this statement do you say that Mr. Milutinovic said to you that bombing Serbia would lead to massacres. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the statement. When I reviewed our daily dispatches --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Nowhere in the statement --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Then you testified in the trial of Mr. Milosevic in 2002 and you gave a detailed account of this evidence regarding Mr. Stambuk and that's Exhibit P2793, pages 7232 and 7233. And I'll read to you what you said under oath in the Milosevic trial. The question is: "And what, if anything, can you share with the Court about negotiations as expressed by Mr. Stambuk?" And your answer is: "Well, I had several -- of course, we had many, many, how should I say? - one-on-one meetings, informal meetings in the "boudoir," at dinner or breakfast or wherever in Rambouillet. And on one occasion, Vladimir Stambuk, and we were discussing, he was a member of JUL. And when we were talking about -- when I was referring to the necessity to ensure the implementation of this agreement and for this we need, in order to demilitarise the KLA, international military presence. And if this is not granted, then we will reach the end of our negotiations." And then Mr. Stambuk basically said, "Well, if there is bombing of then this will -- it will mean a massacre in Kosovo. And of course it was -- I was quite impressed to say the least by this. It was very clear to me that he was referring to a massacre on the part of the Yugoslav Army or the MUP on the Kosovo Albanians. We did not -- I -- since I was taken aback very much and shocked in a way, I did not further elaborate, but it felt -- it left me in the distinct impression that there was a clear view, at least with Mr. Stambuk. What would happen if there was a war or bombing in Kosovo?" Now, nowhere in your testimony in the Milosevic trial did you say that Mr. Milutinovic said to you that bombing in Serbia would lead to massacres; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this exchange between you and Mr. Stambuk. What comes out of it is that you're discussing the necessity of implementation, demilitarisation of the KLA, otherwise, negotiations will end. And Stambuk says, Bombing will lead to massacres. Now, in this courtroom, on Wednesday, at page 10728, let's compare the details with what you said on Wednesday with what you said during the Milosevic trial. Here's the question the Prosecutor asked you a couple of days ago: "In the context of these discussions you were having at the time, what did you understand him to mean?" Him being Stambuk. Your answer is: "Well, it was very clear we were talking about the military component of the peace accords and it was clear that if, unless we are successful, there is going to be an NATO activation order and we, the negotiators, will be out of the game. So it was. It became very, very clear at the time that either we reach a peaceful agreement with -- set out in the proposal, including a military component in order to - as I already said - secure a safe and security environment in Kosovo for all its people there. And second, to be able to demilitarise the KLA, which is part of the agreement. Unless we succeed, there is going to be another main actor which is NATO, clearly. In response to this, Mr. Milutinovic, President Milutinovic at the time, said that: "That that would definitely lead to massacres," meaning on Albanians in Kosovo. "This is my understanding, I should add." Now, sir, I put it to you that you are mistaken when you say that Mr. Milutinovic said this to you; it was, in fact, Mr. Stambuk, not Mr. Milutinovic and your memory has failed you. Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I was -- at the time when I was given the opportunity to talk to the investigators, I had very much on my mind this episode with Mr. Stambuk. Now, when I received those documents, my dispatches to Vienna, I was reminded that the same was also said by Mr. Milutinovic in one of the many, many conversations and the two, I must say, were not the only ones. That were -- that was also a logical and understandable reaction to say, okay, something's going to happen, you know, massacre. And, as we know now in retrospect, of course, this is exactly what happened when the NATO intervention took place. We have numerous massacres committed by the Serb security forces during the NATO intervention on the ground in Kosovo. So I mean this is -- that was logical that, at the time, that they said this will happen, and indeed, in fact, it happened. So I don't know why you now believe that this is not correct. It was Mr. Stambuk who said so, that is documented in my testimony, and it was Mr. Milutinovic who said so, which is documented in one of my dispatches to Vienna. Immediately after the dispatch was sent out, immediately after several hours after this meeting with Mr. Milutinovic, without any thought of -- I don't know, now, accusing someone. This is a totally internal dispatch and was of course not written to be discussed anywhere, any time in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, let's break this down. What I'm suggesting to you is this: When you met the Prosecutor in May and June 1999, three or four months after Rambouillet, he was asking you specifically about -- about Mr. Milutinovic, among other people, specifically. Now, you knew Mr. Milutinovic. You say that the declaration by Stambuk made an impression on you and I believe it did.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, if Mr. Milutinovic had said that to you, in those words, you would not have forgotten; that's the point I'm making, sir. You're an intellect man, we're four months after the fact and I'm putting it to you --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg to disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think what is now happening, if one looks at the question, is that he was going to put -- break it down and put a simple suggestion, fact by fact, or whatever. It has now become purely argument -- argumentative suggestion -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing wrong with the question. Please carry on, Mr. O'Sullivan, and complete it hopefully without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If we look at the context of that statement, the Prosecution, two weeks later indicted Mr. Milutinovic and they were looking for any information that people would have had. And they were asking you, What can you tell us about Milutinovic and you never mentioned this. You said Stambuk did it. And you said it made an impression on you. And I'm saying that you would not have forgotten. I'm only suggesting that you are mistaken and we'll come to those -- that exchange of your dispatch in a moment. But it should be -- I'm trying to impress upon you that it would be logical for you to remember three months later who said what and particularly when you knew Milutinovic and you were dealing with him and you were shocked by Stambuk's statement, not by Milutinovic's. That's my point. If you can allow for the fact that maybe you're wrong about this.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg to disagree. Clearly, at the time when I was interviewed by ICTY, obviously, this one example came to my mind and not Mr. Milutinovic's example. Once I re-read the dispatch, I was reminded that the same had happened also in a conversation with Mr. Milutinovic. You need to keep in mind that this was a very intensive times, very intensive three weeks. They are day and night negotiating. So sometimes you're more impressed than other times. You remember some episodes and you forget others. I was reminded on this Milutinovic incident by my report, which I filed immediately after -- obviously after this meeting with Mr. Milutinovic. That's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All I'm suggesting is that if these words had been spoken by the President of Serbia, they would have made a strong impression on you; and the reason they didn't, was because they were not spoken by Mr. Milutinovic. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your point but it is not my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there the possibility that there was a mistake made at the time of the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I must say that that is very, very unlikely because you would not just write -- put something into writing about the president, the acting president, or the president of a republic, part of then-Yugoslavia, if it were not said, particularly in such a dispatch. It's an internal dispatch, again I must reiterate, and, of course, we as diplomats are bound to say and write the truth and nothing but the truth. That is clearly one of the main principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's explore this a little bit more, Judge Bonomy's question. This dispatch that you referred to is P562, and you saw it in your testimony here at page 10729, lines 20 to 24. You say you saw this dispatch for the first time last week when you came to testify here, some eight years after Rambouillet; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you -- the dispatch is at tab 28 of your materials. P562. Now, you did not --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Tab 28, please.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to my dispatch now?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I've confused you. In fact, I don't think I have it in -- it's not in hard copy, my apologies. We have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it P562?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: P562 is on the screen, sir. Do you see that? That's the --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see that this -- you did not draft this document, did you? It was your assistant, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. It was -- it was in all likeliness my assistant, Mr. Kickert. And I would also like to point out that the meeting was also attended by Ambassador Mayorski. Now you can imagine, sir, if I would have written something or approved something where there were other witnesses, in particular, Mr. Mayorski --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, there's been no suggestion made that you're lying on this. If we get to that, that's another matter. All that's been suggested is that there's a mistake made. Now, I think perhaps you're addressing an issue that's not presently before us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So this document was drafted by Mr. Kickert; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor in May and June of 1999, and I can represent to you, that on the cover page, Mr. Kickert is present with you on the 14th of May. He's there.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, at no point did he say to you, remind you, or come to you at a break and say: "By the way, Ambassador, don't forget about what Milutinovic said about bombing and massacres." He never said that to you, did he?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if we look at the top of this document, we see that it's sent from your embassy in Belgrade to Vienna; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was received as an encrypted e-mail document because that -- this was the only way for us to communicate with my head office in Vienna via encrypted e-mail via -- it only went via Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. And it --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was only possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it was sent from Paris to Belgrade then to Vienna; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reflecting the status of the 20th of February, 6.00 in the morning, it was.
