utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A person named Mr. Senfter?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Senfter was at the time working at the embassy in Belgrade, an Austrian diplomat, who basically forwarded this again encrypted to the head office.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this document was -- is dated 20 February, 0600 hours, so it would have been prepared by Mr. Kickert just before sending it, just before 0600 hours in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: During the night.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So this document passed through two sets of hands, Mr. Kickert's and Mr. Senfter's?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at page 10730, lines 2 to 7, you said this about these internal reports: "They were internal reports, ad hoc reports, not covering the entirety of the process in Rambouillet, clearly, because we had other means of communication, telephone," and so on and so on. "It was, of course, a very turbulent time, so these reports are very much ad hoc, very much written immediately after the event but not in a systematic way." Sir, what I'm suggesting is what Judge Bonomy has pointed out to you, that there's an error here. It was produced in the middle of the night or in the early morning hours by Mr. Kickert. There's a mistake in this document. Your memory was only refreshed after eight years, you say, from seeing this document a week ago. You spoke about it, Mr. Stambuk, three months after Rambouillet in the presence of Mr. Kickert, you've testified under oath, and you never once, never once attributed these words to Mr. Milutinovic, and I'm suggesting to you that you misspoke, that you -- that what you say jogged your memory, in fact, is not correct, that you would never have forgotten if Mr. Milutinovic said such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's asked and answered two or three times, repetitious, and argumentative. That's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I put the question in the full context, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're all agreed that this question -- the answer to this question will assist us, and we'll therefore allow it to be asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such a massive insinuation or accusation, as is expressed here in this dispatch, I am convinced that this -- there is no mistake. It was said as was put into this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you if you remember the actual circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a meeting with -- together with Ambassador Mayorski and we're talking about -- it was the 19th in the evening and we were talking about the whole issues, that this was the last evening before the supposed end of the conference. So clearly, that was -- that was a very, very tense situation and the issues clearly were on the table, and that was the military implementation part. And also what if the negotiations failed, then we would have reached the end of our diplomatic path. And we knew at the time -- everybody knew, including Mr. Milutinovic, of course, that already since early October of 1998 NATO had issued the activation order, which I already explained what that meant. So the Damocles sword of NATO was dangling above our heads, and these were the circumstances under which this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you actually now remember it or are you rationalising that this must have been said because it was recorded in circumstances where we are bound to tell nothing but the truth, as you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You actually do remember it being said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I recall when I read this, then I recalled the circumstances and that it was -- I can also attest to the fact that whatever has been put into such reports, it was of course, as I said, not an integral reflection of the conversations but more, so to speak, the highlights. And, obviously, one of the highlights was intransigence, no progress, and the threat by Mr. Milutinovic that in case NATO takes -- NATO intervenes, then there are going to be massacres in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- if you look at what's appeared on the transcript, that suggests that you don't actually remember it being said, but you're satisfied -- convinced in your own mind that it was because you can recollect the meeting and you can recollect the circumstances of it and you know the way in which these matters were reported. Have I got it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's time to break, but I don't want to interrupt you at this minute if you want to pursue that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Why doesn't your diplomatic correspondence mention Mr. Stambuk?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated before, not everything was mentioned. We just went into this. There were hundreds, if not thousands, of meetings in these three weeks, you know, and of course we first and foremost wanted to drive the negotiating process forward. And these reports were basically taking some of the issues and reporting them back to my head office. That was basically it. So it never covered -- as I indicated, it never covered the whole of the meetings which sometimes took place almost 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So despite being so shocked by Mr. Stambuk, that didn't make it into your report?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over time one gets less shocked by what has happened, you know, unfortunately, and less impressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We'll -- we can break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll break for 20 minutes now, Mr. Petritsch, as we have to, and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00. If you could again leave with the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, there's a mistake in the transcript. I misspoke at page 29, line 10. I said P2260. It should be 2660.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake also in one of the page references to the transcript from the Milosevic trial, because the witness didn't give evidence for five or six days, which would be necessary for the two page references you gave to make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll review that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I didn't have a chance to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May we please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can attempt to clarify it now. The page references I wanted to give you were 7232 and 7233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 7232 and the second page is 7233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Bonomy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was a slightly earlier reference, reference to P2793.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there was a transcript reference that I've recorded as 7726, but it can't be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll have to check that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Ambassador, dealing with the Rambouillet process I'd like to ask you this: Is it your position that the Rambouillet process was conducted in a transparent way and that all documents that formed a part of the agreement were tabled to the parties?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents were tabled according to the prior agreed way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the process was transparent. Would you -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the process was transparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: To be clear, there were no documents, no agreements, no side deals, no side letters that were not tabled. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- as I have already indicated, there was once the attempt on the part of the US to issue a side letter, and that was then abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So your position is that there were no side agreements, no side deals?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit P2260 is at tab 39. 2660. I made the same mistake. 2660, tab 39. It's your dispatch to Vienna dated the 22nd of February, 1999, at 0900 hours. It's a document you looked at yesterday quite extensively with my learned friend, Mr. Stamp. And I'm looking at the -- just to set the context for my questions. You see there that you've described that: "The situation in Rambouillet took a dramatic turn for the worse from 21 to 22 February." Then we -- you have the reference to the stubborn insistence on the referendum issue and the Kosovar intransigence regarding the dissolution of the KLA. Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on page 1? Are you referring to page 1 or page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Tab 39 for you, the first page.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First page.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you see that? Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document now, but I did not see the sentence that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph. It begins: "The situation in Rambouillet took a dramatic turn for the worse."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in there you highlight two problems, the referendum issue which has existed since Saturday, and the question of the intransigence of the KLA to dissolve itself or --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- to demilitarise.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph begins: "Gef," that's you the undersigned, "had a last meeting with the Yugoslav Serb delegation at 2.30 in the morning. The only points remaining open were the review clause and minor Kosovar comments on the wording for procedure when the vital interests of national communities are under threat. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So this is a meeting you had, then, with the Yugoslav Serb delegation on the Sunday, the 21st -- sorry -- the morning of the -- in the wee hours of the morning --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the wee hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So we're about a day and a half after the meeting on the 20th with the Contact Group foreign ministers.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 20th they were summoned into the room with all of you, both delegations, we're about a day and a half later; correct? And -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat that. I was not fully --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: To put this in time.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On Saturday, the 20th --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- is when the --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- foreign --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Contact Group foreign ministers --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And here we are --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To get the yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Here we are about a day and a half later --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- in the wee hours of the morning with the Serb delegation?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we're still -- the Serbian position is still general acceptance of the political components at this point, correct, as reflected in this document in the paragraph I just mentioned. The only points remaining open were the review clause and minor Kosovar comments on the wording for procedure with the vital interest of national communities --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- are under threat. So we're in the same position, general acceptance to the political framework --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- correct? You have to answer for the transcript, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then if we go to the bottom of that first page we see that the real problem at this point, at least, at 9.00 in the morning on the 22nd is the Kosovar delegation. You write: "The agreement of the Kosovars is still more questionable at the present moment in time." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it right now, but it sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Last paragraph, first sentence on that first page.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yeah, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That was, in fact, the situation at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That was the situation? At this point --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- on the morning of the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday, as you saw with my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, in the middle of this page we have the reference to the -- right near the bottom of the page the reference to the Albright side letter?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Surroi came to you and asked for -- whether the EU could provide a side letter?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit is 1D18, e-court page 449. And for you, Ambassador, it's tab 40. Do you have tab 40 in front of you, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Left-hand column, do you see draft for chapter 8, article 1, sub 3, 22 February 1999, 0525 hours and proposed draft side letter. The first paragraph of this letter contains the language of the then-proposed chapter 8 of the Rambouillet agreement, and below that is the text of this letter. And the letter states: "This letter concerns the formulation attached above. Proposed for chapter 8, article 1 (3) of the interim framework agreement. We will regard this proposal or any other formulation of that -- of that article that may be agreed at Rambouillet as confirming a right of the people of Kosovo to hold a referendum on the final status after three years. Sincerely, Madeleine Albright, Secretary of State." This is the letter that your dispatch referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And your dispatch states that -- that's P2660, the one at tab 40. It states: "The Kosovar delegation was informed by Albright, among others, that the referendum and continued existence of the KLA were out of the question" --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now referring to the dispatch of February 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You want me --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to explain the process --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You explained that letter was withdrawn and the position was made clear that there would be no -- that this side letter would not form part of any agreement?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the European position which I proposed and maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And staying with this exhibit, your dispatch of the 22nd of February, you write that -- at the end of that document, second page, last paragraph, it says: "Several concomitant measures were agreed upon to ensure a positive decision by the Kosovars. And one is a warning that various measures would be taken. Even a US statement to put the KLA on the list of terrorist organisations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So what we're saying here is that the Americans were telling the Albanians, If you don't sign, then one of the consequences may be that the KLA would be put on the American terrorist list. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that Mrs. Albright had told the Kosovar delegation that if they signed the agreement and Serbia did not, that Serbia would be bombed?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So you learned about that later?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after the end of the conference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So let me see if I've understood the position in relation to the proposed side letter. This letter was a personal initiative of Mrs. Albright?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it was not supported by the Contact Group, the EU, Russia, or even the FRY delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the letter was withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So the understanding at this point is that the Contact Group and the EU had considered, unacceptable, a side letter concerning assurances of a referendum after three years. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back to your testimony yesterday, and it's something you said at page 10741 and 10742. You were testifying about the proposed side letter in response to a question by Mr. Stamp, and it's the side letter and the question of a referendum. And you said: "Now, when the American side said they would be ready to issue a side letter, we Europeans were totally opposed to it. The Kosovar Albanian side wanted now -- they found out that the Americans would be ready to sign such a letter, then they said, Why don't we also need this from the Europeans? And they said to me, Mr. Petritsch, we want a letter from the European Union to the same effect. And I was absolutely against it and I knew this would be backed up by the European Union, by the European Union Presidency, Germany at the time, so in that -- in the end we succeed." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And also during your testimony, you were talking about a whole question of a referendum in the Balkans and how it -- as you put it, if I can paraphrase it, a referendum is a powder keg in the Balkans, it's a recipe for disaster. Is that a fair way to put your -- summarise your views on that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As was proven in the past, I now was referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Powder keg, not potter cake. It's a powder keg. Can we have P2659 on the screen. That's your e-mail dispatch of 23 February, 1999, at 1230 hours. I'll have to find the exact reference here. Well, it begins at the bottom of that page and I want you to explain something to the Court. Do you see the last sentence Hill and Gef, you, the undersigned?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So here we are at 23 February, 1999, 1230 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And go down to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "Hill and the undersigned offered the Kosovars -- were offered the following approach to resolving their problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Second bullet point: "A unilateral statement that the Kosovo delegation has interpreted 'will of the people' as a referendum, the results of which will have to be taken into consideration when deciding about the final status of Kosovo." Now, Ambassador, would you please reconcile the fact that you and Ambassador Hill were suggesting a unilateral declaration and referendum when you consider a referendum to be a recipe for disaster in the Balkans. Tell us how you can reconcile that.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. First and foremost, the goal was not to have the expression "referendum" in a legally binding international accords. That was our first and foremost goal. Secondly, we, of course, realised that nobody can prevent anyone from organising a referendum, and this is the unilateral referendum which has no legally binding relevance. That is the reconciliation that you were asking me. We told them that if you decide later on to hold a referendum, we cannot prevent you from doing so, as we cannot prevent Serbia from holding a referendum about Kosovo. So this is a legitimate instrument in any democratic system. This is what this expresses. I am very, very much interested in making this point very clear. If there would have been a -- let's now think in these terms. If there would have been a referendum in Kosovo, clearly one knows what the outcome would have been. Yeah. Close to -- or maybe over 90 per cent in favour of whatever the referendum says. If there would have been a referendum in Serbia, the same would have happened with the opposite result. So this is why I say, out of my own practical experience in working in the Balkans, working in ethnically dominated societies, that this does not make sense to have one; but secondly, one cannot, in a democracy, prevent anyone from organising a referendum. The decisive issue is the status of such a referendum. If it were part of the Rambouillet Accords, it would have a higher legal relevance. And if it is done as part of expressing the will of the people, of course, it would have been taken into consideration, but not as a binding decision because -- and that is the reason why we broadened this final clause and included - as I've already said and I'd like to repeat it here - the Helsinki Final Accords, the Paris declaration, and all the other accords regarding the CSCE and there, of course, the principle is no change of borders with military means or, in a positive way, change of borders only by peaceful means. And in this way, of course, we have balanced, in this final part of the accords, the decision which would have been taken later on by an international meeting. So we made sure that this is a fair and balanced formula where the two would have to come and find a compromise. And in case, theoretically speaking, in case that formula would be independence, it would be accepted if reached by negotiations between the two sides, Belgrade and Pristina. I'm sorry to be a bit longer, but I think it is very, very important to stress this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excellency, I have a question to ask. I'm from the Bench. Now, how would you, under these circumstances, place plebiscite or the right of a nation for self-determination? Would you have opposed that or you thought referendum was an answer to that? Because there was a right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And how would you dilate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly there is a right and this was -- this is expressed in all sorts of international and legal documents, but that was not the point there. We had a very clear framework of autonomy for this. This was the goal of the Rambouillet Accords, but since it was an interim accord, clearly there needed to be in there a provision how do you proceed after the interim is over, so to speak, after three years? And that was the formula that we found a compromise where we thought and are still convinced that both sides are included in there and that these two sides have, in a democratic way, figured out, with the help again of the international community, what the final status of Kosovo will be. And if it's -- if the Kosovar Albanians claim the right to secede, this international meeting needs to deal with it and the Helsinki Final Act has to be taken into consideration. The will of the people has to be taken into consideration. The achievements in these three years in terms of democratisation and so on need to be taken into consideration, particularly the rights of the minorities, particularly the rights of the Serbs and all this stuff. By the way, this is a very appropriate discussion right now because, right now, this very same discussion is on about the future status of Kosovo, but that's another story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: How would they have expressed without there being a plebiscite or a referendum? How would you have determined that then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That can be done in very different ways, but including the referendum. But we did not want the exclusive right to be the referendum as the decisive factor. That is the most important thing, because the same would have applied to the Serbs. They could have organised in their country - and Kosovo is part, formally, and in these accords, part of Serbia, part of Yugoslavia - and they, of course, could have organised a referendum as well. And as I said before, the outcome would have been very different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is something that I think I have failed to understand here clearly. The reference to the will of the people in the bullet point that you've been addressing, we saw yesterday in a later version of the proposed back letter -- or side letter. Is that correct? That's where this expression comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will of the people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Or have I misunderstood that? You've told us that the side letter had been withdrawn by this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where was the expression "the will of the people" to come into the accord?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think I can be of assistance if it's -- it's in evidence. We're dealing with the 18 February version of the Rambouillet Agreement and it's chapter 8 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The language is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, that version includes the expressed will of the people. The final version does not include the word "expressed." The final version, being the 23rd of February, chapter 8, it says "the will of the people." The 18th of February had the word, "expressed will of the people."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we toned it down. That was upon the Contact Group to eliminate the expression "expressed," so tone it down to the will of the people, and not as the Albanians were asking, the expressed will of its people. So these were the two changes that were made, the two demands that we did not accept from the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But yesterday we saw that the side letter contained that expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the side letter is at tab 40, it's 1D18, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was its role then in these terms at that stage? So at tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Tab 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 40. Yeah -- that's not the -- that's not the -- these are not the terms of the side letter as we saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We didn't see the side letter yesterday, Your Honour. We didn't see a side letter yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What we had yesterday was the dispatch for the 19th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, which quoted the proposed terms of the side letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not the side letter, the proposed terms of the agreement presented on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, right. I'm sorry. I have misunderstood the contents of that -- I'm sorry about that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chapter 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Your Honour, if you look at tab 40, 1D18, page 449, you see the paragraph within Mrs. Albright's side letter, "three years after the entry into force."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph is in chapter 8 of the 18 February version of the Rambouillet Agreement and it includes the word "expressed will of the people." And that -- in Ambassador Petritsch's dispatch, yesterday, we had that text. And to complete the picture, the final version of the Rambouillet Accord, 23 February, contains this paragraph without the word "expressed" in chapter 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the exhibit number of the dispatch? Tab number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the dispatch that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me a tab number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 39. Yes, Your Honour, tab 39, and you see on that first page there's a blank spot where it says "text in English." If you recall yesterday, we had to look at the German original because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the text was already in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's understand the position. The -- why was the -- the side letter by Mrs. Albright you have said was vetoed as being unacceptable to the Contact Group, to the EU, and Russia because it brought in an interpretation of the expressed will of the people by telling -- by assuring the Kosovar delegation that in three years the people of Kosova could hold a referendum. That was the problem with that side letter; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So why is it that knowing that, why are you and Ambassador Hill a day later suggesting to the Kosovars to go ahead and put that into their unilateral declaration?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot -- this is what they said, Okay, then, we are going to put this into our declaration. And I said, We cannot prevent you guys from doing this. That's -- I think logic directs us to say, Okay, we need to accept this as we accept this from the Serb/Yugoslav side to say no referendum and here was, Yes, referendum. But it was for us of the ultimate importance not to have the expression "referendum" in the Rambouillet Accords because then, as I say, it would have had a much more official meaning than to say, rather, will of the people and define it in a much broader way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Why weren't you repeating to the Kosovars the assurances you gave on the 10th of February to the Serbian side that their sovereignty and territorial integrity would be preserved and say, Don't do this, this is leading to a problem? Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, I already said, three times in at least, if my recollection doesn't fail me, the territorial sovereignty and the -- territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is included in the Rambouillet Accords, starting out with the preamble. I think we really went the extra mile in order to secure something which, at the time, was absolutely the opinion and the conviction of the European Union and the European states. We wanted to preserve the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Yugoslavia. You can believe us, for us Europeans, to go with this ever more dividing and atomising the Balkans, this is not a solution for us, because at the same time, Europe is integrating and not being divided with yet another province and so on. So it was for us very clearly the position we do as much as we can to preserve the integrity of the already-reduced territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm talking about 1999. I know later on Montenegro left and now there is a wholly different game on, but at the time that was our stated position.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit 1D18, page 467 -- 476. That's at tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the top left of that page is the unilateral statement or declaration by the delegation of Kosovo, 23 February, 1630 hours. Do you see that at tab 41?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, that is the declaration that was made by the delegation on that last day at 1630 hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the last paragraph, first sentence: "The delegation of Kosova understands that this would be confirmed again upon signature," meaning they will come back in two weeks, "and at the end of the interim period of three years, Kosova will hold a referendum to ascertain the will of the people as provided in article 138 of the chapter of the agreement." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe it's page 467 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this is the -- this is the declaration you say that came out publicly in the afternoon of 23 February, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the closure of the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now -- let's move to Exhibit P2658 --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- which is your final report to the foreign ministry on 25 February, 1999. And I'll just read a short section to you. So you sent the report to Vienna on the 25th of February, two days after the end of the conference?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was done already in the ministry in Vienna, because I see Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs up there which basically means that -- because we left Rambouillet on the 23rd in the evening, I guess -- 24th in the evening, I don't know, but anyhow that is not a dispatch from Rambouillet but was then written on -- what is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The date is the 25th, I believe, at the end of --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 25th, I believe by Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And there's a section on basic agreement. On the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, for being a little lost here. Second page. You can go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Bullet point, right in the middle of that page it says: "Basic agreement on the Kosovar side for unilateral declaration." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "Which was achieved after a chaotic and dramatic final session in which Hill exclaimed: Do you want NATO or not? And in which Surroi and Thaqi first signed at 1620 hours." Now, that's a reference to the unilateral declaration; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is basically to sign up what the -- let me re-read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting, if I could help you --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, what this is is -- yes, it is referring to this -- to this unilateral declaration at 1620, but it is not part of -- we wanted to get from them a declaration that they would be ready to continue to negotiate after the resumption of the conference, as we did in the letter of the 23rd of February at 16 hours from the Yugoslav/Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: To be fair to you, the unilateral declaration does say they're ready to continue --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and to sign in two weeks.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was for us the relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what I want to pick up on here is this chaotic and dramatic final session --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- which you highlight there. Did you know that during this chaotic and dramatic final session that a side letter was prepared by the Kosovar delegation and that the side letter was addressed to Mrs. Albright personally concerning a referendum to be held by the people of Kosovo at the end of the three-year period. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since it was dramatic and chaotic, you have to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know about the letter I've just described, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You knew about it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about it later on but it was a bilateral dealing between the US government and the Kosovo delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had nothing to do with the negotiating process.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, but probably in the later -- probably after the end of the conference or whenever I went through and recollected the information and the material in order to put together this first impressions after the end of the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, there's no reference in your materials to the letter I'm referring to, the one addressed personally to Mrs. Albright from the Kosovar delegation --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's not in there. So therefore I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You just told me you did know about it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I asked you, when did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Shortly after the conference, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much shortly after the conference, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that this letter -- or did you know that Chris Hill and Jim O'Brien from the state department were present and participating with the Kosovar delegation in drafting this letter?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that Jim O'Brien was blocking Hashim Thaqi's access to his interpreter's computer while the letter was being drafted, not allowing Mr. Thaqi to see the text?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that Veton Surroi signed this letter, the personal letter to Mrs. Albright?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that question has been answered three times already, Mr. O'Sullivan, because the witness makes it clear he doesn't even know the letter exists until after the conference was over. End of story.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's a short video clip I would like to play. The video is Exhibit 1D206 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It relates to these events in the final -- it relates to the events starting on the 20th of February through to the 23rd and this creation and signing of this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are these events that the witness is likely to know about and be able to comment on or are you doing this for show?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm doing it because I've asked him whether there were any side agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Any -- and whether the side agreements were vetoed or not by the EU and Russian and Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And whether or not the Rambouillet process was transparent and whether or not there were side agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is this going to add to our knowledge of the number of side agreements that seem to have been around?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, it won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, it will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's going to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it goes to perhaps the credibility and bias of this witness his -- he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm -- okay, but if it turns out this is pointless, then obviously we will have to have regard to that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- term --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But please continue for the moment and then we'll assess the position but we will have regard to how the time is being spent. We have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I fully -- I appreciate your comment, but I would not be presenting something that I considered pointless if it's -- it's fundamental to the fact of the allegations against the participation of my client in this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please proceed. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- as presently advised going to stop you from doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The film is Exhibit 1D206. It's an excerpt, in fact, from Prosecution P771 and P771 is the BBC documentary, "The Fall of Milosevic." We have a transcript which is 1D205 and that's at tab 43. Now, according to your directions, we have had this transcript reviewed by CLSS, and I can state to the Court that it's been approved by CLSS. There are Albanian, French, and Italian speakers. Those are the sections that have been reviewed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 42, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 42. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 42. And you'll see there that the shaded portions are the speakers who are not speaking English and that has been reviewed by CLSS. I can say that the subtitles in the video are accurate. And I'd ask that the video be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "Narrator: After two weeks of hard bargaining the foreign ministers arrived for the final session. They summoned each delegation in turn. "Madeleine Albright: The foreign ministers all sat at a long table as if we were in judgement or something. And first Thaqi was brought in with a couple of other members of the Albanian delegation. "Hashim Thaqi: [No interpretation] "Madeleine Albright: The question was basically: Do you agree with the framework, yes or no. And we were expecting a yes, or I was. "Robin Cook: He needed further improvements, and of course, the improvements we wanted were ones that we knew were unnegotiable, they were impossible to get agreement on. And eventually I had to say to him, look, the real -- the bottom line here -- the real question is: 'Can you say yes to this package.'. "Veton Surroi: [No interpretation] "Lamberto Dini: [No interpretation] "Hashim Thaqi: [No interpretation] "Madeleine Albright: He kept kind of moving around the issue and when he wouldn't say 'yes' I remember taking off my earphones and putting them down on the table in just pure exasperation. "Lamberto Dini: In particular she didn't like my insistence -- [No interpretation]. "Madeleine Albright: I thought that the way that the language had been constructed provided what in diplomacy we call some creative ambiguity. "Lamberto Dini: [No interpretation] "Madeleine Albright: And Dini got more and more insistent and said: 'Are you willing to give up independence?' "Veton Surroi: [No interpretation] --'This is what I told you -- I told you so.'. "Hubert Vedrine: [No interpretation] "Lamberto Dini: [No interpretation] "Narrator: For the cameras, Mrs. Albright stuck to her usual line. "Madeleine Albright: The Serb delegation bears the lion's share of the responsibilities for the difficulties we have experienced today. "Narrator: But in private with Hashim Thaqi she took a different tack. "Madeleine Albright: I said, Look, I don't understand what just happened in there. You have let us down. Ah, it is an impossible situation now. How could you do this? We expected you to be a leader. "Hashim Thaqi: [No interpretation] "Madelaine Albright: You could see that he was just shocked. I mean, he looked like a high school student that I had dressed down. "Hashim Thaqi: [No interpretation] "Narrator: The Kosovo Albanians were given three more days. They wanted to sign, but they were still under pressure from the gunmen back home. For 72 hours, they did not leave the castle or go to bed. As the deadline approached, the delegation was still arguing. Then the American negotiator went to their room. "Chris Hill: I said, Guys, we're there now. We've got five minutes now to really decide this thing. "Veton Surroi: [No interpretation] "Chris Hill: I said, So are you going to sign this thing or are you not? At that point, Surroi spoke up. "Veton Surroi: [No interpretation] "Narrator: Veton Surroi had a brain wave. The document they were being asked to sign said, 'In three years an international meeting would consider a final settlement for Kosovo and the will of the people would be taken into account.' Surroi suggested they could sign it if Mrs. Albright accepted a letter stating that the will of the people would be tested in a referendum. "Veton Surroi: [No interpretation] "Narrator: Thaqi was trying to read the draft on his translator's computer screen. "Dukagjin Gorani: And I have Jim O'Brien and Jamie Rubin behind telling me: 'Hurry-up, man, hurry-up, he can read it later.' "James O'Brien: And Thaqi is saying, 'maybe you can change that.' And I said, 'No, no, you can't change.' And I began to step in front of him and sort of bump him back away from the computer. I want it done. "Dukagjin Gorani: And Thaqi becomes tremendously nervous and says, you're not leaving this chair until I get both wordings in both languages. "Hashim Thaqi: [No interpretation] "Dukajin Gorani: O'Brien just takes the sheet of paper, knowing that if the paper remains a few more minutes in Thaqi's possession he would probably change his mind. "James O'Brien: I said, 'Jamie here's a copy - you're going to announce this.' "James Rubin: I thought that I'd better first check with the Secretary of State and I snuck into the conference room and whispered in her ear what had happened and she said, 'go out and announce it.' "Narrator: The letter was addressed to Mrs. Albright so she was able to accept the referendum compromise without consulting her colleagues. "James Rubin: Then I really started to get my blood pumping and I began running through the hall in that crazy castle and out through the gates, and into the town square, to finally tell the reporters something good. 'Very briefly, the Kosovar Albanian delegation have voted in favour of this agreement - pending consultations with the people of Kosovo.' The Albanians had chosen peace - and deferred independence- and the Serbs had not. And, now, there was the clarity that the world needed in deciding whose side they should be on. "Narrator: With a referendum in the bag Thaqi won over the commanders back home. The delegation returned to Paris for the signing ceremony. Milosevic stayed home, claiming foul play."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you've told us that at the time you had not seen this letter that the Kosovars addressed and sent to Mrs. Albright. Did you see it subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At tab 41 -- where was it you saw the letter then?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But, again, would it be shortly after the conference, does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much after the conference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, it's tab 41, 1D18, page 467 -- 467. You see it on the left-hand side of the page letter from the delegation of Kosovo to US Secretary of State Albright, 23 February 1999. And I'm looking at the second paragraph: "We want to convey to you our understanding on two points. First, we acknowledge your view that the agreement allows and does not preclude a referendum in Kosova which will demonstrate the will of the people in Kosova and which will be conveyed to the international meeting to be convened to determine a mechanism for a final settlement for Kosova, as called for in Article 1 (3) of chapter 8." Now, isn't this letter just a mirror image of the letter that the EU and the Contact Group and Russian Federation has vetoed as inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you said you knew about this letter after the conference, and I'm asking you -- and you told me this was a transparent process. Why did you say it was transparent if you knew this letter was out there?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the three negotiators. I'm talking about the process, the Rambouillet process, I'm not talking about activities that were outside of our realm. We had a very clear mandate what we needed to do, but we were not there to reign in individual foreign ministers. We did not do this with Madeleine Albright and we did not do this with the other ministers including the Russian Foreign Minister Ivanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Fair enough. We're sitting here in 2007, Ambassador, and I'll be more specific. Knowing what you know now and what you've seen, you would agree with me that there was a side letter, a side agreement, coming from the Secretary of State of the US and that this process was not transparent was this was never made public, was it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is -- obviously was made public in this documentation; and secondly, we -- this was not part of our mandate. We had -- this is also not part of the Rambouillet process. This never went into the official documentation of the -- of the Rambouillet Accords. So therefore, I'm not in control of -- of maybe some of the side letters of any of the foreign ministers present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch -- well, before I address anything to you, so far I remain unconvinced that that has done anything to advance our knowledge of matters that could not have been done simply by the questions that you're asking and by reference to the documents. Now, if I can address a particular point to Mr. Petritsch. Part of the process we've heard was a threat on behalf of the United States that failure to sign could result in bombing of Serbia. If the back letter or side letter was an essential element in securing the agreement of the Kosovo Albanian delegation and thus pinning ostensibly in the public eye blame for the collapse of the Serb will to sign and thus leading to the bombing of Serbia, you will see that it might be argued that the ultimate process, not the way in which you did it, but the overall process contained an element that wasn't transparent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Your Honour, that we're talking of the 23rd of February, and that was the date that both delegations, the Albanian and the Yugoslav delegation, provided us with a written information that we were asking from them. And that is to continue after a hiatus of two to three weeks to negotiate the implementation. And that was also expressed in the Contact Group's statement of 23rd of February by the foreign ministers where it is clearly stated that the civilian and the military implementation parts need to be negotiated after the resumption of on the 15th of March. Undersigned by all the foreign ministers of the Contact Group. So that was the important thing. On the 23rd, nobody was blamed that the process is faltering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not even the Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm not understanding at this stage is the idea that you -- well, the impression you were under that you were -- had achieved a commitment by the Kosovo Albanian delegation to the further process, which you would not have obtained but for that side letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is now pure speculation. I don't know. But the fact is that they agreed, that they agreed to what we -- what we had proposed and that they informed us they would continue to negotiate. We're talking about something which, of course, is much further off. This is the 23rd of February and there both sides agreed to continue on the 15th of March and, very specifically, on the implementation issues of these accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, how much longer will this cross-examination last?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's rapidly nearing its end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I would refer everyone to IC126, which is the table that I distributed this morning that lists the contents of the Rambouillet Agreement over the period of 6th February, 18th February, and 23rd February.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, you -- I believe you have that document in front of you, do you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The table. Perhaps the usher can give it back to you. It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm now dealing with the right-hand column, and you see there that the final text of the agreement 23 February now includes chapters 2, 5, and 7, the implementation chapters; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Rambouillet Agreement is P474, Your Honour, but I am proposing Exhibit 1D98, which is also the Rambouillet Agreement, but it includes a cover letter. So I'm not trying to clutter the record with two versions or two copies -- identical versions -- two copies of the Rambouillet Agreement, but the important point in 1D98 is the cover letter which is at tab 43 of the hard copy materials. So for the sake of clarity, 1D98 is the cover letter and the full text of the Rambouillet Agreement. That's in the e-court system which you have at tab 43 as just the cover letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Ambassador, what you're looking at -- do you have that at tab 43?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What you have there is the cover letter signed by the troika dated 23 February 1999, 9.30 a.m. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And here you are sending the integral Rambouillet Agreement, all nine chapters, including chapter 4A, and the second paragraph says: "The final proposal takes account of the views expressed at the Rambouillet meeting. Russia does not associate itself with chapters 2 and 7. The co-chairman and negotiators are ready to receive your response no later than 1.00 p.m. today." And we see that Ambassador Mayorski signed it and he wrote in his hand "except chapters 2 and chapters 7." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the table IC126, if you look at the right-hand column I've also put the pagination of my exhibit 1D98 preamble, one page, the framework, page 2 to 6, chapter 1, pages 7 to 25, and so on. It's an 81-page document, as you can see by looking at the bottom of that right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it's an 81-page document, Mr. Ambassador, and chapters 2 and 7 together amount to 47 pages. Over half the documents are tabled at 9.30 in the morning, not approved of by Russia, and you're asking for the views of the parties by 1.00 the same day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What's incorrect about that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. The implementation chapters, as we had already stated over the past two days, were handed over on the 18th of February --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's stop there --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's explicitly --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's stop there --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is explicitly mentioned in one of my dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's look at that.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Because I explicitly challenge you on that, Ambassador, that is incorrect, and I'll show it to you; all right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were interviewed by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on the 27th of February, this year, a couple of days ago. And you said this in your statement a couple days ago. "The implementation and military sections, including the annex B, were handed over to the Yugoslav side on the 18th of February, 1999. I am not from a NATO country and Christopher Hill focused primarily on the implementation issues, including the military component. My understanding is that he handed it over to them at that time." So the first point I want to make is that it's your understanding based on what Ambassador Hill told you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at P563. That's your dispatch of the 19th of February at 1300. That's at tab 37. Do you have tab 37? Do you have that, tab 37?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is P563. Here's what you wrote at the top of that page: "Annexes 1A, military and police" -- sorry: "Annex 1A, military, and 2, police were transmitted to the Kosovar delegation on the afternoon of 18 February. Opinions still outstanding, apparently because translation not yet complete." There's no mention there of it being translated to the Serb delegation, is there?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this dispatch, but that was clear, as I expressed before, that it was Chris Hill who handed it over to the Yugoslav side, and they rejected to formally accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page of this dispatch. Middle of the page. "On 18 February, annex 5: "Civilian implementation was finally agreed within the Contact Group and with the OSCE. It empowers both the OSCE and the EU to engage in civil implementation. It will be put to the Kosovar side today, 19 February." No mention of it going to the Yugoslav side, correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is a wholly different story. This is an internal discussion between the European Union and the OSCE, who is going to lead the civilian implementation mission; that has nothing to do with the -- what you just insinuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we also know from your testimony, that on the evening of the 19th of February, that's the Friday, members of the Kosovar delegation met outside the castle with Wesley Clark to discuss these very points; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have mentioned this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you agree?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about it, yes, there was a meeting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit 1D97. 1D97 at tab 44. 1D97, tab 44. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by Professor Markovic, head of delegation, to Mr. Vedrine and Mr. Cook. Let's look at it. 22nd of February. "Today's meeting with a part of the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia was announced as a meeting of experts for the exchange of information about the comments on the agreement on self-government in Kosovo and Metohija. However, this meeting was used for an attempt to hand our delegation for study papers which have not been adopted at all in the Contact Group." I put it to you, sir, that this shows that the documents which have not been approved by the Contact Group are, as the letter -- your cover letter shows on the 23rd, chapters 2 and 7. And this --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- letter suggests that they were tabled -- or handed to the Yugoslav side on the 22nd of February, not the 18th so --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I beg to differ. They were handed over on the 18th, very clearly, sir. But there is another issue. I just want to remind you that I, throughout this testimony, I said that this Rambouillet process was divided into two parts. The first part was to finish up in Rambouillet the political part, negotiating, getting the formal approvement of the two sides and the Contact Group and so on and so on. The implementation issues 2 and 7 and 5, by the way also, they were already scheduled to be dealt with after the interruption for three weeks and then starting on the 15th of March, we would have taken these to discuss and to negotiate it. That is the reason why Mr. Mayorski indicated this in this cover letter. There's a very logical reason to it. And since this was not yet approved and harmonised in the Contact Group, foreign ministers' meeting, it could not have been presented as a harmonised proposal. But we were only looking and that is expressed clearly in the letter of the 23rd by the Yugoslav side that they are ready to continue to talk about -- to negotiate about the implementation part of the -- there is no -- no -- nothing whatsoever what are trying to insinuate has -- is of value in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, when they were handed over, as you say, on the 18th, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- and this is also indicated in one of my dispatches that they so to speak -- they took it, but they said we formally -- what we want to know you formally now that we do not accept it. This is not that we have received -- this is -- we do -- we have not formally received it, so we are not going to deal with it. That was, by the way, the reason why, after the 18th, we moved closer and closer to the fact that we will have to interrupt and then have a second meeting in order then to concentrate -- to focus on the implementation issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why was your communication of the 22nd of February confined to saying that these chapters had been given to the -- sorry, the communication was the 19th, was it. Why was it confined to saying that these had been given to the Kosovar delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because this was -- are you asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we reported what was there something that the -- the military part, the implementation part is very important for the state clearly. Yeah. And we can only negotiate with the state such Status of Forces Agreement. A non-sate actor, as I've pointed, in this case, the Kosovars, do not have a role in this. And to them it was provided one day later on the 19th for information purposes. That was also the reason, obviously, for the meeting with General Clark that Mr. O'Sullivan just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I would just read in this context a sentence from P979, that's at tab 30, but I'm just going to read the sentence to --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This is P979, tab 30. It's the statement of the Contact Group of 29 January, 1999. The one where they summon the parties to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, January, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The last sentence in paragraph 4 says: "It," the Contact Group, "required that the parties accept the level and nature of international presence deemed appropriate by the international community." Now, Russia forms a part of the international community, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: An important one?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And they have not agreed to this annex 2 and 7, had they?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you want a response by 1.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we see a letter --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: A response to the question: Are you ready to go on with the negotiations starting on the 15th of March? That is to be a bit more broad in explaining what this all is about. This was not about accepting something which was not yet negotiated, which was not yet agreed in the Contact Group. So you are focusing on something which does not have relevance in this context that we are talking about and this is the 23rd. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I beg to differ with you. We saw the letter of the 22nd where the delegation says, we are not -- these are not papers. They are not approved by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's a meeting convened by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the articles or the chapters 2 and 7, also 5, were not agreed yet in the Contact Group. This is the implementation part, and therefore, consequently, the resumption of the conference on the 15th of March was devoted to this and we wanted to get a positive nod from both sides to agree to this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, in spite of all this, P625 is a letter that Professor Markovic sent to you on the 23rd, that's at tab 45, where he's stating the position of the delegation, that they are prepared to discuss the scope and character of an international presence.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's in the fourth paragraph. In the third paragraph he says: "All elements of self-government at the time of the defining of the agreement have to be known and clearly defined."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. But you, yourself, have said that this represents a positive, constructive approach by this delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At this point I have to remind you of something which I -- which you've said, which I challenge as well. And I digress for a moment. P2792 is your interview with the Prosecutor, the one that you had in May and June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1999, yeah, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there you -- and we've established that Mr. Milutinovic arrived approximately on the 11th of February, end of that first week; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You said this to the Prosecutor: "Milutinovic was not part of the Rambouillet delegation and his arrival marked the end of any constructive effort to find the political solution." Now, you misspoke there; didn't you? That's not correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a reference to the resumption of the conference on the 15th of March when basically Mr. Milutinovic took over and was the spokesperson of the Yugoslav delegation. Mr. Sainovic, who up till then and Mr. Markovic did a job throughout the Paris leg of the conference. These two gentlemen never ever spoke. It was always Mr. Milutinovic who spoke. And that was after the decision, obviously, was taken on the part of Belgrade. And I would say in parenthesis, "Obviously, I would suggest by Mr. Milutinovic [sic] that it's the end for a constructive engagement." We are going to continue now with an obstructive approach and that was the task of Mr. Milutinovic in the Paris leg of these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe there's a mistake in the transcript at line 22, page 86, I believe the Ambassador said Mr. Milosevic not Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
