utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Line 22?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're right, Mr. O'Sullivan. The reference in line 22 was to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You said Milosevic and there's a mistake in the typing.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So to be clear, then, your position is that Mr. Milutinovic was constructive during the Rambouillet period?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Rambouillet, the -- he was not -- as I said, he came later on, but he was really engaged and fully also as part of the delegation only in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you've said that there were three letters that day presented to the troika by the Serbian delegation?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: E-court 1D18, page 466, tab -- for you, tab 46. We have all three letters there. Tab 46, e-court 1D18, page 466 of e-court. Do you have that, Ambassador? Tab 46.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 46. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom right-hand portion of that page, number 33 is the letter that we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The letter at 1600 hours. And what I want to emphasise here is that this -- this letter in the middle paragraph says: "All elements of self-government at the time of defining the engagement have to be known." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the first letter --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to put it -- making reference to the political part which was already negotiated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Now, the reason I want to show you the other two letters, and particularly the first letter, which is number 31 on that page, which is the lengthiest one. There the delegation has not included a -- any reference to a continuation on the scope and character of the presence -- of negotiating that part; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's no -- I can tell you there's no reference to that in that first letter --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This was the reason why in my meeting with Mr. Sainovic I politely pointed out that this would be no -- amounting to a no, and thus the fail of the conference. So Mr. Sainovic then immediately went back and then they produced a new letter at 1430 and then this one -- this second letter was followed by a third letter that you have just referred to without actually our instigation because the second letter already contains the key word of "implementation and the continuation," but still we got a third letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the reason I'm directing you to this first letter is because it does spell out in some detail the delegation's position on what has been accomplished --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and what's left open, in regards to the political framework. If you look at -- if you go -- we don't have to look at all the bullet points and I certainly won't. We see a list of bullet points, nine bullet points, setting out where the delegation says that there is agreement. However, there are some -- in the next paragraph, after the bullet points, there are a number of matters throughout the rest of this letter regarding the constitution, the decision making in the Assembly, the President of Kosovo and Metohija, the judicial system, constitution, property, et cetera, which needed refinement and further improvement; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So the Contact Group was fully aware of the position that the Serb delegation took in relation to the political components. There was general agreement, and here the areas for future discussion from their perspective are spelled out; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The second letter I will not --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I comment on the first letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, yes, I think this was a very detailed letter, pointing and spelling out what was achieved and where this is agreement. So -- and then the -- the second part of the letter goes into spelling out where there is no agreement yet. Now, what are these examples? The example are -- is, for example, the expression "constitution." The Yugoslav/Serb side maintained, throughout the conference, the expression "constitution" is reserved for a sovereign state, so therefore, it should not be used in this context. That's a linguistic and a legal issue which you can of course discuss forever. I'm sure within -- we would have been able to find a solution within -- at the end. Again, I have to remind you, nothing is agreed unless everything is agreed. So therefore, that is one of the points. The second point is president of Kosovo. They did not like the expression "president" for the president of Kosovo. They wanted something else, chairman or something like this. So these are issues that of course you can discuss for hours on end and you will not reach a solution unless there a compromise. And I'm confident, if these would have been the only problems, we would have very successfully succeeded and concluded the negotiations there. So this is not really a valid point that the -- the Yugoslav side was not -- was not basically agreeing that there is agreement on the political side.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My point is quite the opposite, is that there is basic agreement from the Yugoslav side and that these are points of refinement which need further discussion?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, but as I said, this was not contrary to the general gist of the discussions and on the 23rd to say in -- generally, you have to agree with this, then say yes; and then to the second point, which is the continuation of the negotiations about the implementation chapters. But clearly we can re-visit issues, contentious issues like whether you call it president or chairman or constitution or basic law and something like this. This is not a big problem. So therefore, you are right. Yes, there was a basic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm nearly completed. I would just like to finish a couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we -- well, within reasonable range of 20 past, are you going to finish? Because if so, we'll go on until you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can finish in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're aware that the FRY was a federal state with a federal constitution, with a Serbian public constitution, federal laws, republic laws, and this sovereign state had to harmonise any agreement it was going to agree to on a part of its territory, giving it substantial autonomy and self-government. So these are all legitimate concerns --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- that are spelled out in this letter --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We very much appreciated this and took this into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were told also in meetings that you had, and you say this in Milosevic -- in your statement, P2792 page 4, you were told in relation to implementation, that more time was needed?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So you were aware of two things, that further, specific refinement that are legitimate for a federal state to want to discuss in relation to the political component were necessary and more time is needed to discuss implementation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And yet, when you come back to Kleber in Paris, the Serb delegation is told, No, you're only here to discuss implementation. No discussion on the political framework; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. May I explain again? You, of course, give now the three weeks. The prime factor was a very important one now at the end of Rambouillet for both sides. The KLA part of the Albanian delegation -- Kosovar Albanian delegation was panicky about the -- how will the KLA reach their commanders and this -- how will they react to the dismantlement of their organisation. That was the one point there. And on the other hand, of course, you had the problem in -- on the Yugoslav Serbian side, how do we now explain to our citizens that there is going to be a military component in this agreement. And that was very appreciated by us. This is a difficult part for any government to convince the people, to convey to them, that this is something that we will then sign up to. And the Contact Group foreign ministers, therefore, asked the three negotiators to travel to -- both to Belgrade and to Pristina in order to discuss the remaining open points, the ones that you just mentioned from the political part, and of course also implementation issues. How is this going to go? How are we going to organise it? And so on. So the three weeks were used by us for intensive meetings and dealings with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you came back for the three days in March, in Paris, and the Yugoslav delegation wanted to discuss the political component, they were told, No, it's final; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- we said, We first need to do the -- what was agreed at the end of Rambouillet, the implementation issues, and once we have successfully finished the implementation issue, that was on the agenda for the second meeting, we would of course be ready to go back -- to come back to the political thing and then -- but for the time being, we are not going to do this. This is for practical reasons. We need to finish. And whether it's called president or chairman does not bear any relevance in regard to the implementation issue. And only if we successfully finish negotiations about -- concerning the implementation issues, the issue of president or chairman will be relevant. If we fail this issue - and as we now know we failed - this issue will not be of relevance. Why waste time on something that can be decided at the very end in a very short period of time? That was the reasoning that we clearly conveyed through the Contact Group, ourselves directly to both sides. Because, of course, also the Kosovar Albanians wanted something else here and there and so on. We said, No, this is finito. We need now to move on what we agreed on the 23rd and these are the implementation chapters.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now you've reversed everything. Now you're saying implementation comes before the political part. Earlier, you were saying the political part must be --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is misrepresenting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Stamp. What the witness's position on this is quite clear, Mr. O'Sullivan, and you can make submissions on it in due course if you think he has contradicted something he said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- I have very little but perhaps we should take a break -- maybe we should take a break if it's important for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is, but we have another witness to have in mind today and I've already tried to establish whether additional time will be available for that if necessary, and hopefully it can be arranged. So your time is not limited and we can have the -- that's subject to everyone being willing to cooperate on that. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I have two brief areas, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you wish a break now, we'll take it. But I thought if we completed you, we would then be able to judge the rest of the day's timing better. But if it's going to be more than a couple of minutes, then we'll need to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I have some indication of how much cross-examination there will be from other counsel? Who has questions? Mr. Fila, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly less than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half an hour, a lot less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than that: 20 minutes, 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us not bargain on this. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've had one of them already. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Roughly, 15 minutes. Maybe up to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that is it as I understand it; is that correct? Mr. Stamp, is there much re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So far, not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it clear that witness -- the next witness requires to give evidence orally and be cross-examined? Is that an essential part of that witness's evidence? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We definitely have to cross-examine that witness and I can say now that we will not accept the approach that that witness took in Milosevic trial when she refused to answer further any questions. So if the Prosecution wants to put that witness on the stand, we expect her to answer every and single of our question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but how long is that likely to take, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's plain, that to achieve the completion of both witnesses we'll require both time than would be available, if we finished at quarter to 2.00. We can go on for one more session after that with an appropriate break, which would be at least three quarters of an hour. I hope that there would be willingness to do that with that particular witness. We initially had in mind the possibility that we could go even further, depending on what happened this morning, but that's not now going to be conceivable. So hopefully we can go that far in view of the sensitivity that is felt by the witness, rightly or wrongly, I think we should respect it nevertheless and try to get through her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are ready to stay as long as possible. Probably my colleagues would stay -- wouldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, I understand that you have some opposition to state to this. Just before you begin, I don't think we need to detain Mr. Petritsch. Meanwhile, he can have his break. We'll be resuming -- well, you'll be told when we'll resume once we complete this debate. If you could, meanwhile, go with the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't spoken about time for a long time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but can I make my position clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think your position is clear and I'm preparing to withdraw my objection because it seems to have something to do with getting a witness taken care who, otherwise, would be here for a long time and I sympathise with that, so I'll gut it up and stay with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova has had to depart for urgent personal reasons unexpectedly, and therefore we will continue without her; we consider that to be in the interests of justice, bearing in mind the stage we've reached with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The final document I'd like to look at with you is P2658, which is in e-court only, 2658. Ambassador, this is the final report that you prepared on the negotiations. You've seen this before with both Mr. Stamp and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of the second page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, which tab is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's not a tab. Look at your screen, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Top of the second page you report this in that first bullet point. "In the final analysis, the negotiations verged on failure. Such a failure had to be avoided at all costs, not only for co-chairman Cook and Vedrine, but also and especially for Albright, who had invested her whole prestige (her critics noted that her presence for days on end and the stubborn resistance of Thaqi made her participation 'trivial')." Now, you reported -- this report accurately reflects your view on the fact that, especially for Mrs. Albright, her prestige was on the line; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody's prestige of course was on the line and since Secretary Albright was actually not a formal part of the -- of any of the negotiating teams or the co-chairs, as by the way Mr. -- President Milutinovic on the Yugoslav side, it was clear that by her high-profile interventions that her prestige was connected with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I guess it would be fair to say and you would agree that she assured her prestige by accepting the side letter from the Kosovar Albanian delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I -- you would have to ask her. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on page 1 of this same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we go down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's a -- the second-last bullet point which is on the screen in part 1, the one that begins: "Strong European components..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "Strong European components in the negotiations (venue, co-chairmanship of Cook/Vedrine, EUSE)" --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "Towards the end, in particular, however, the USA tried to take over the negotiations (Hill's trip to Belgrade, presence for days on end of Secretary of State Albright in Paris and Rambouillet); prominence of the significance of PR," which you've told us is public relations; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Ambassador, you wrote to your foreign ministry, failure had to be avoided at all costs. We've heard Mrs. Albright say and Veton Surroi confirm this in this courtroom that if the Albanian sign, they Serbs do not, then NATO will bomb. And if all this happened, then there would be clarity and the world would know whose side to be on. Isn't that what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me again remind you that this is a report about the first leg of the negotiations and it reflects the first part of the Rambouillet process. So there, failure had to be avoided under any circumstances is a bit of a phrase, of course, but it just said that we had to go the extra mile in order to achieve this result in Rambouillet by getting from both sides the go ahead for the second round.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellency, my name is Toma Fila and I am Defence counsel for Nikola Sainovic and I am going to keep my word, and I'm going to use up even less time than I said although -- anyway, what the Court allowed me. Excellency, I would just like to dwell on page 7 of your statement and I will only restrict myself to questions related to Mr. Sainovic. Paragraph 1 on page 7 of your statement in the English version, that is what we are going to deal with now. In it you said that at one moment towards the end of 1998 Sainovic was appointed the Envoy of the FRY in Kosovo. I would like for you to have a look at a document, that is 2D8.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, it will be there, but I'm just asking you so we don't waste any time. When you see the document, please answer this question very briefly. Is that what you were saying that had been sent, once you see the document, that is. That is the decision, yes, the decision on the formation of the commission of the federal government for the cooperation with the OSCE mission. The government of the FRY appoints Mr. Sainovic the chairman of that commission. That is paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the document that you meant?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. -- [In English] No, actually, what I referred in my report was - if I would have it in front of me then I could quote more precisely --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not your report, not the report. Sorry for interrupting you. Your statement to the Prosecutor, page 7, paragraph 1, the statement you made to the OTP, that is what I'm talking about. We're going to deal with your reports later, but you've just had a look at this. Is that what you had in mind? Do you have your statement in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it -- I have it in front of me, but I was not referring to this specific commission of the federal government for the cooperation with the OSCE mission for verification in Kosovo. My information at the time was that since the summer of 1998, Mr. Sainovic was in charge of Kosovo. Yeah. This document I cannot recollect, but I assume that that was a consequence of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, that this commission was formed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to deal with something else, but we will go back to what it was that you just started just now. If you look at paragraph 2 of this decision, do you see that the task of this commission was to coordinate the political security and logistical aspects of the functioning of the OSCE mission, so that would have been Sainovic's role; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this context, obviously, because it's in writing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, we are going to talk about what you started speaking of a few moments ago. Could you please look at 2D16 now, dated the 7th of October, 1998. That is the document you're going to see right now and that is supposed to support your position, namely, that even before this appointment, he was made in charge of Kosovo. So I would like you to look at this document now and does this really show what his line of work was? You have it now, and what I want to ask you is: Regarding the content of this document, does it correspond, more or less, to your telegram, the one that was sent with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read it, but it seems to cover this same meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what specifically are you now referring to? What should I comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, nothing --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you whether this is what you meant when you said that he was in charge of Kosovo, that he had this task. So he had the authority of the Government of Yugoslavia to discuss Kosovo. You will agree with me on that. I'm trying to cut this time as short as possible for you. What I want to ask you now is: Is it your assessment that this meeting -- show that he was useful to you at this meeting because that is my conclusion on the basis of the fact that you invited him for dinner afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that as a matter of rule, all the meetings, as opposed to other meetings with other representatives of your former government, all the meetings with Mr. Sainovic were positive in the sense that it was -- these were always decent meetings, based on mutual respect. There I'm including the meetings -- the frequent meetings which we had in Rambouillet, and therefore it was, of course, of use for me and I also had the impression that Mr. Sainovic was listening and trying to respond. You need to keep in mind October 7th, that was at the height of the October crisis prior -- a week prior to the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke. So it was a very good atmosphere personally and was something which I still remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that there was also a meeting sometime around the 29th of December, this same year, 15 ambassadors were there and you headed that group. This was a meeting with him and that meeting was useful, just like you mentioned a few moments ago about the other one.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sainovic, of course, always -- as this is the de voir of any functionary to -- he put forward the government position, but it was a useful meeting again in a very decent atmosphere, considering the fact that we were in the middle of real deep crisis in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you for these kind words, Mr. Ambassador. Now I'm just going to ask you something else and we're going to be even quicker. You mentioned in your statement paragraph, 6 on page 7 in the English version, the incident that had to do with the soldiers that were taken prisoner and, on the other side, the KLA soldiers when you said that you vested your personal authority in having this done. And you say, if I understand this correctly, that Sainovic was the negotiator to whom you conveyed this and then this happened and then he said to you that it was the president who had decided on that, he probably meant Milosevic. Do you agree with me that Sainovic could not have made a decision on this but it was Milosevic who had to make the decision? Is my understanding of what you said correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm sure that Mr. Sainovic proposed to Mr. Milosevic to decide in a positive way on this, and in this way again it was a constructive - how should I say? - it was a constructive move on the part of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show a document to you, 2D16 -- no, that's not it. Sorry. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D15, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you take a look at this, it has to do with a meeting in Vienna. You see the date, the 7th of October, 1998. No, no. Yes. Let's just see it. If you remember, it has to do with Mr. Sainovic's visit to Vienna. The date is the 5th of January, 1999. At the end of the document you can see who the attendees were and you were there as well. Can this meeting also be characterised as a useful meeting?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You remember it, yes? Various principles were referred to there. The Trial Chamber can read this for themselves. We can see that it has to do with human rights and respecting the human rights of all in Kosovo, not to have any out-voting and so on and so forth. When we look at this document, I come to the conclusion that a high degree of agreement was reached between you and Mr. Sainovic regarding the resolution of the crisis, that is to say through political means and peaceful means. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with this in regard, again, to the date. That was prior to -- to the massacre of Racak or the Racak incident, and up till then we still had a lot of hope that we -- it would be able -- it would be possible to reach a peaceful agreement based on KVM and the instruments that were in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, you know what gentlemen we are, the Serbs, so the rest of your time is on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law, one of the Defence counsel for Vladimir Lazarevic, and I have a few questions for you. First of all, my first question has to do with part of your statement that you gave to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in 1999. Do you perhaps have this statement in front of you or do we need to have it on e-court?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please provide P2792 on e-court, page 6 of the English translation, the one-but-last paragraph. The English original, to be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, in the one-but-last paragraph, the second sentence, you say that during the March meeting in Paris you received reports that Serbian and Yugoslav forces were active in Kosovo. Military action had taken place in and around Vucitrn and a military offensive was already underway in Kosovska Mitrovica. Mr. Petritsch, can you tell me who it was that you received this information from?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] These were in -- this was information which we received from intelligence sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what intelligence sources?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be more specific on this, but it's -- the way it is said here stands correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, if I were to say to you that the verifiers of the Kosovo Verification Mission were on the ground in Vucitrn touring other areas and that that is not as is stated in your statement, or rather, that it is in contrast to that report, would you allow for the possibility of this report that you refer to being incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I do not know the KVM report, of course I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I were to say to you - and we heard the testimony of high representatives of the KVM here who were on the spot, in Vucitrn - if we have different reports here that say that in Mitrovica there weren't any clashes or conflicts, would you allow for the possibility that what I've been saying is correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to allow me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to answer this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is rephrasing the previous question, but it's -- calls on the witness to speculate about something he doesn't know about, about KVM documentation. He has already said where he got his information from, which is the base of his knowledge and the base of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, were you going to add anything significant or were you going to say that there's a limit to what you can answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's -- unfortunately, I cannot contribute anything to this question because I'm unaware of those sources that were quoted by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am referring to sources that we heard in this courtroom during the course of this trial, primarily the KVM --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can look at these as contrasted with the evidence of Mr. Petritsch. All he's saying is he doesn't know what the contents of these reports were and I suppose he, like me, in this situation would say anything's possible, but that doesn't help advance the cause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petritsch, during the Paris negotiations did you perhaps receive any reports about the KLA, starting with urban terrorism in Kosovo, planting bombs in towns where there were several casualties, the 13th of March in Mitrovica, to give a specific example and not to give any further examples. We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, with referring to your specific example that you have given now, of course the 13th of March was prior to the resumption of the second part of the conference, but nevertheless, yes, we were very much aware that this is not a one-sided exercise, that both sides clearly are in part, at least, when it comes to the Kosovar Albanian side, resorting to force. That was the reason, by the way, why we had to rush and sometimes be a bit rough, also, with the negotiating team because we feared that there would be a relapse into conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely in that period during the Paris negotiations, did you perhaps receive OSCE reports from Kosovo that it was the KLA that intensified attacks against civilians, the police, and the military during the negotiations and during the course of the negotiations? I'm referring to Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall the specific source, whether it was KVM, OSCE, or something else, but in general, that is when I recall my feeling at the time was that the situation on the ground is deteriorating and that we need to speed up and come to a conclusion in these negotiations then, particularly in the second half in Paris. And may I add here one episode. We were sitting in Paris negotiating and Mr. Milutinovic, as I said, has taken -- had taken over the lead of the Yugoslav delegation and we were involved in sort of totally useless --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, sorry for interrupting, but with your permission, I asked you about sources from the OSCE -- or rather, the KVM. I asked you whether you received reports from them, so then let's not waste time. If you don't have information from there let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking if the witness could finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It didn't seem, though, it had anything to do with the question with respect and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't insist on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. And equally, Mr. Cepic, unless this is leading to something that you think the witness can tell us about, we know there's evidence about the KLA's actions around March, and all you're getting is answers from the witness that merely say I don't know or both sides were at it together, but if it's coming up to something significant, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour, by your leave, I just wanted to hear whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mr. Petritsch had that information. That's it. I have no further questions regarding that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a point, though, to be made, though, on this in general that whether he heard about KLA activity or not may not really have any significance at the end of the day. I mean, I thought perhaps you were coming to some point of significance in his -- in the role he played because he had heard of KLA activity. I think your source of that evidence is elsewhere. Anyway, move on to your next point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask the registrar for P2793, the transcript of Mr. Petritsch's testimony in the Milosevic trial. 7240 is the page I want.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, my colleague Mr. Fila touched upon your mediation with regard to the prisoners in January 1999. I would be interested in the following: You stated during your testimony on this particular page --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Line 22, that's where it starts -- that it was early January 1999 a group of VJ soldiers were taken hostage by the KLA and in turn a group of KLA people were then taken by the VJ and there was a situation where you were asked to help and mediate the release of these two groups. I would be interested in the following: How did you come about this information that the Army of Yugoslavia had taken a group of people who were KLA members for this exchange, as you had stated?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was quite a celebrated case at the time that the KLA had taken hostage a group of Yugoslav soldiers and then that there were, of course, efforts underway on the part of the international community in order to defuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know a great deal about this already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there's a particular question being asked, which is what's your source of the information that the VJ acted in retaliation by taking hostages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say retaliation. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was incurred that it was just -- I would say the time-sequencing was such, and I found out through our contacts with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what would you say to me, Mr. Petritsch, if I were to put something to you that was confirmed from several sides in this courtroom that these KLA members who were exchanged through your mediation are actually KLA members who were arrested on the 14th of December, 1998, on Mount Pastrik at the border between Yugoslavia and Albania in a border incident? Meanwhile, the VJ soldiers were kidnapped on the 8th of January, 1999, that is to say considerably later in respect to the first incident.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only convey to you what I have learned. It might as well be the case as you have just described it, but this is not the main point. The main point is that we tried to negotiate with both sides to get -- and it was explicitly said by the Yugoslav side, not in an exchange, but there was a flexibility on the part of the Yugoslav authorities, particularly Mr. Sainovic to say okay, let's try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- let's try and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Mr. Cepic's line is rather different --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- from the other -- his interest is entirely different from the other two counsel who cross-examined you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he's much more concerned about the actions, not the diplomacy which followed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, but I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we have heard a lot about the exchange from people who were involved also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can refer, of course, and report on the diplomatic side on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not on the military side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petritsch. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp. No one else has questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, at various points of the cross-examination you were asked about ostensible efforts made and you were shown documents indicating that invitations were set out by Dr. Markovic and sometimes by Mr. Milutinovic in 1998 to the Kosovar Albanian side, so to speak, to convene meetings and at one point you said that there were reasons - and you referred to reasons on various occasions - as to why the Kosovar Albanian side could not be expected to attend. And I think you referred to, without finishing your answer, the backdrop of political and the security situation in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- where it could not be expected in those circumstances that there would be these types of bilateral meetings the Yugoslav authorities ostensibly were convening. Could you fully explain why in the political security and historical setting that occurred.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically this was done during the time when on the one hand we saw these declarations and the ostensible offer to negotiate and to meet, and on the other hand the security operations on the ground were ongoing and in particular, of course, it was also a reflex of the fact that after the massacre in Milosa in -- where the Jashari family was basically wiped out, there of course, was a total refusal on the part of the Kosovar Albanians really to get involved, although later on Rugova tried, because he was the one who went the extra mile to try, and of course, but on the militant side, on the side of the rebels, there was simply no readiness to allow the political establishment, so to speak, to talk. That was the problem. And this was very clear to everyone who was involved in it, that this is not the right way to find -- to find something that we wanted, and this is a meeting. And we suggested time and again to the Yugoslav side, Please find other venues to forge a -- such a meeting, because we were, of course, supportive of such a meeting. But just by announcing you're going to get an invitation and then you get an invitation, that is -- was at the time not the way to handle. This you can do with friends, but in a conflict should have deployed different diplomatic means in order to reach this desired meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to the statement that you recorded here in Exhibit P562 about what Mr. Milutinovic said. Can I just ask you, this document, this e-mail dispatch, you had told us briefly how they were created. I'd like you to answer this specifically: Who would have written this dispatch, and that's 562.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I again have the number?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: P562. Yes, I've got it. That was written by Mr. Kickert and approved by me. Usually that happens that there is a draft and then I go over the draft and make some corrections, if necessary, stylistic or otherwise, sometimes it's too long or something like this, because we wanted to be precise, but of course, it's fully under my authority that this has been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, it refers to -- to the meeting this the chateau on the 19th of February --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- and at the heading it says "re: FRY Kosovo Rambouillet negotiations at the 20th [Realtime transcript read in error "28th"] of February at 0600 hours." Can you recall - and if you can't, just say so - approximately how long after this discussion with Mr. Milutinovic would this document have been?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to tell, but I would suggest that that must have been more towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall what time in the day it was that you had this discussion with Mr. Milutinovic in the chateau?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it was in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's been answered. There's a mistake in the transcript. It's the 20th rather than the 28th of February that should have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question I should have -- I meant to ask you earlier and, I'm sorry, I didn't. What language did Mr. Milutinovic use when he made the remark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what language did Stambuk use when he made his remark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I should say, Mr. O'Sullivan, if you want to come back on that, you'll be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the language, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In respect of it, yes, since I've asked a question here that he might wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not that I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked him that in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you ask him about Stambuk as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So he's had his opportunity. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I'm asking a question which has been answered before. There has been a lot of material and I think I might have forgotten the answer about the time when he spoke with Mr. Milutinovic at the chateau on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said a moment ago, approaching evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late afternoon/early evening, so approximately -- but I cannot be absolutely sure, but somehow when I recall the scenery, so to speak, then it must have been more towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. How long after the meeting between General Clark and the Kosovo Albanian delegation did you discover that this meeting had taken place?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't -- I don't recall. I'm sure it must have been not too much later, a couple of hours or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. There were quite a few foreign ministers at Rambouillet, including the -- Mr. Ivanic from Russia --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Ivanov. Mr. Milo, I think, his name is, from Albania, and of course was from France, Britain, the United States. And you said that there were side letters -- or there was an issue raised in respect to side letters. Did you have any control or did yourself or any member of the troika of mediators have any control over the meetings that these foreign ministers could have with various members of the two delegations?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. The Contact Group foreign ministers felt free to meet with whomever they wanted to meet, in particular, the two co-chairs, since they were the political -- politically responsible for these negotiations and all the others, Mr. Ivanov, Mr. -- of course, Secretary Albright. We spoke at length about Mr. Fischer from Germany, representing the EU Presidency. And that was basically the format. The Contact Group foreign ministers took the liberty to speak to anyone they choose to speak or we made proposals who should speak, who should approach one of the two delegations, or individually speak like to Mr. Milutinovic or to Mr. Sainovic or to Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Rugova and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, these side letters, how would you assess their value in terms of binding force in comparison to what you hoped to achieve, achieve the ultimate final agreement between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what's important is that the means that were employed outside the troika format and not agreed within the troika was one thing. The other thing was - and this is what counted and was formal and binding - what the troika did and said and what was of course also approved by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown a video, and I don't intend to go over the video with you unless you need to, but the transcript for the video is among the documents that you were given. It's in just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's tab 42, yes. Whether I may ask you and you could consult the tab if you want to answer. Were you a party to and that is present and participating in any of these meetings and discussions that is referred to in the video?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was -- I mean, as this is expressed here, this was an episode that these -- this documentary, I guess it was this BBC documentary, dealt at length with, but it was this aspect of, so to speak, document in minute detail how the Kosovar Albanians acted, so to speak, in these negotiations in this very -- at this very point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the video refers to various meetings and discussions between members of the American team, team of the United States, and Mr. Thaqi and Mr. Surroi. Were you present and participating in any of these?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the specific one, but in general, yes. I had of course also contacts with all those that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you not present at the final session meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's the one -- that's the one of the contacts there that you were actually a witness to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there of course at the formal Contact Group meeting of the foreign ministers, but in this documentary, there was, of course, also the issue of how within the Kosovar Albanian group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when the Albanian representatives who were described as three were brought in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you were there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excellency, while going through one of the documents on the e-court, I saw one of your reports which suggested that you had been meeting Mr. Milutinovic at different places, but your first meeting with him in Belgrade, where you spoke also, led to a bit of acrimony because you reminded him of The Hague Tribunal or talking of The Hague Tribunal. Now I was wondering, why did you think of The Hague Tribunal at that time in your Belgrade meeting of October. And then later on, you said that Mr. Milutinovic has been talking about things pertaining to this issue whenever he met you. Could you kindly dilate and clarify this position. I'm thankful.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, correction, that was not Mr. Milutinovic whom I addressed, but Mr. Milosevic in his capacity as president of Yugoslavia, and Mr. Milutinovic was present and in his then-capacity as Yugoslav foreign minister. And you are now referring to my -- when I presented my credentials to President Milosevic, and in this -- in this short speech, I also referred to cooperation between the necessity for the cooperation between Belgrade and ICTY. And then later on in the meeting, in the sort of private meeting that usually takes place after the presentation of the credentials, then Mr. Milosevic came back and sort of -- but there I do not recall what he said, but clearly it was not something which was welcomed by Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milutinovic, to my knowledge, did not react at the time to my speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But, what was the necessity at that time talking about this Tribunal while you went for a very formal function or presenting your credentials? I mean, what was in the back of the mind?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the necessity that was expressed invariably in all the meetings with Yugoslav officials that, in order to fully re-establish diplomatic relations between the international community and Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia needs to play by the rules. And one was, of course, was cooperation with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, that completes your evidence. Whatever else might be said about it, it was extremely interesting to listen to. We are grateful to you for returning to the Tribunal to give evidence again, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, we have available to us, if we choose to use it, about an hour or so this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the general agreement that we could try to deal with the evidence of the witness in about an hour? It would depend on the chief being fairly brief. Do you have much, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can do that and return here at five minutes to 3.00. We'll have an hour's break just now. Obviously, that's the normal routine when the interpreters are stretched and we need to use the same interpreters this afternoon I understand, so we need to give roughly an hour's break. So we'll return at five minutes to 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
